content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, October 30, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Cancer High-risk HPV common among asymptomatic rural Ugandan women by October 26, 2026 in Cancer Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 High-risk HPV common among asymptomatic rural Ugandan women Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A cross-sectional study of 7,126 women aged 30–49 years in rural Uganda found that 1,800, or 25.3%, tested positive for high-risk human papillomavirus (hrHPV). Among the positive women with complete genotype data, infections outside the HPV16 and HPV18 groups were common, while a comparison of genotype groups with clinical assessment found no statistically significant relationship with visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) outcome. The study focused on asymptomatic women who self-collected vaginal samples for testing with the GeneXpert HPV assay. The investigators recorded the presence or absence of specific hrHPV genotypes and used the results to describe genotype distribution in this rural population. All hrHPV-positive participants were invited to receive visual assessment for treatment, with or without VIA, and were treated according to the assessment. No histopathology was performed, so the clinical observations were not accompanied by a histological characterization of cervical lesions. Complete genotype information was available for 1,422 of the 1,800 hrHPV-positive participants. The largest individual genotype group was HPV31/33/35/52/58, detected in 324 women, or 22.8% of those with complete results. Multiple genotypes were the most frequent category, occurring in 397 women, or 27.9%. The remaining distribution consisted of HPV39/56/66/68 in 243 women, or 17.1%; HPV16 in 183, or 12.9%; HPV18/45 in 161, or 11.3%; and HPV51/59 in 114, or 8.0%. These figures show that the detected infections were not confined to HPV16 and HPV18 and that multiple hrHPV genotypes were frequently present. Of the 1,121 hrHPV-positive women who underwent VIA, irrespective of genotype, 159, or 14.2%, had a positive inspection. Eight women, equal to 0.7% of those inspected, were identified as having cervical cancer. Six of these women were positive for HPV31/33/35/52/58, with three also positive for HPV16, HPV51/59, or HPV39/56/66/68. One woman was positive for HPV18/45, and one was HPV16-positive with an unknown additional genotype. The analysis found no statistically significant relationship between genotype and VIA outcome, meaning the study did not establish a statistical association between the genotype categories and the result of the inspection in the population examined. The findings support the authors’ conclusion that the study population had a high prevalence of non-16/18 hrHPV and that extended genotyping may be relevant to managing women at risk for cervical cancer in Uganda. The eight cervical cancers were identified within the smaller group of hrHPV-positive women who underwent VIA; the figures therefore describe findings in that clinical subgroup and should not be read as population-wide cervical-cancer incidence or direct estimates of genotype-specific risk. The authors call for additional research on the possible role of HPV31/33/35/52/58 in cervical carcinogenesis and on whether available vaccines protect the population against the broader range of hrHPV genotypes found in the study. content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, October 30, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health HPV Clades and Age Sharpen Risk Prediction for High-Grade Lesions in AGC-NOS by October 29, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 HPV Clades and Age Sharpen Risk Prediction for High-Grade Lesions in AGC-NOS Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A retrospective study of 588 patients with atypical glandular cells, not otherwise specified (AGC-NOS), suggests that the phylogenetic clade of an infecting high-risk HPV type, together with patient age and infection multiplicity, can stratify the risk of precancerous or worse lesions. The research, conducted at the International Peace Maternal and Child Health Hospital, School of Medicine, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, was published in Diagnostic Pathology and is presented as preliminary evidence pending external validation. The new analysis set out to characterize age, HPV clade distribution and multiple infections in this population, and to build a refined risk prediction model. The researchers reviewed records from January 2019 to December 2023. All 588 patients had undergone liquid-based cytology and testing for 14 high-risk HPV genotypes, followed by histopathologic evaluation. Precancerous or worse lesions were identified in 9.5% of patients (56 of 588), and the overall high-risk HPV positivity rate was 17.7% (104 of 588). The Alpha-9 and Alpha-7 clades were significantly enriched among patients who had outcome lesions compared with those who did not: 19.6% versus 8.3% for Alpha-9, and 17.9% versus 1.5% for Alpha-7. In multivariable analysis, Alpha-7 emerged as the strongest independent predictor, with an odds ratio of 20.43 (95% confidence interval: 7.22–60.07). Alpha-9 carried an odds ratio of 3.41 (95% CI: 1.43–7.57), and each additional year of age raised the odds by a factor of 1.04 (95% CI: 1.01–1.07). The model also incorporated infection multiplicity and AGC subtype. Performance was moderate rather than definitive. The model showed acceptable discrimination, with an area under the curve of 0.74 (95% CI: 0.66–0.82), and good calibration. Discrimination of 0.74 indicates meaningful but imperfect separation of patients who develop lesions from those who do not, leaving room for refinement. When patients were sorted into risk groups, observed lesion rates rose in a graded fashion: 4.5% (8 of 176) in the low-risk group, 8.2% (30 of 364) in the intermediate-risk group, and 37.5% (18 of 48) in the high-risk group, with a P for trend of 6.7 × 10−8. This gradient suggests the model captures real differences in risk across the cohort. The authors concluded that a model incorporating HPV phylogenetic clades, age, infection multiplicity and AGC subtype provided preliminary evidence of potential value for risk stratification in AGC-NOS, with the Alpha-7 clade as the strongest independent predictor. They emphasized that pending external validation, this approach may support more individualized management of patients with AGC-NOS. Several limitations frame these findings. The study was retrospective and single-center, and its results derive from one hospital’s patient population over a five-year period. The reported odds ratios and risk-group rates describe associations within this cohort and do not by themselves establish that clade testing improves clinical outcomes. The authors themselves flag external validation as a prerequisite before the model could inform practice. Within those limits, the work adds a specific technical angle to HPV-based cervical cancer risk assessment: rather than treating all high-risk HPV infections alike, it distinguishes between phylogenetic clades, finding that Alpha-7 types carried a markedly higher association with precancerous or worse lesions in this AGC-NOS population. If validated in independent cohorts, such clade-level information could help identify which patients with this ambiguous cytological result warrant the closest follow-up. content: Skip to content All Regions All Regions BioHealth Capital Region Greater Philadelphia Research Triangle Park News Events Jobs For Employers Sponsorship Log In Sign Up Log In Sign Up North CarolinaIndustry TrendsResearch Waters and Labcorp to Expand Access to Cervical Cancer Screening with the Most Comprehensive FDA-Approved HPV Testing Option Beginning in Late 2026 Published October 30, 2026 · 5 min read · North Carolina ← News / Waters and Labcorp to Expand Access to Cervical... Labcorp intends to be the first commercial laboratory to offer FDA-approved HPV testing with the BD OnclarityTM HPV Assay across clinician-collected and self-collected screening options in clinic, patient service center, and at-home settings Through a network serving more than 850,000 physicians and healthcare providers and more than 2,200 patient service centers, Labcorp is helping expand access to cervical cancer screening nationwide First and only FDA-approved HPV test that supports all ASCCP Enduring Risk-Based Management Guidelines by providing comprehensive extended genotyping MILFORD, Mass. and BURLINGTON, N.C., Oct. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Labcorp (NYSE: LH), a global leader of innovative and comprehensive laboratory services, and Waters Corporation (NYSE: WAT), a global life sciences and diagnostics leader, today announced a partnership to expand access to the FDA-approved BD Onclarity HPV Assay through Labcorp’s nationwide laboratory network beginning in late 2026. Cervical cancer is largely preventable through routine screening and early detection of human papillomavirus (HPV), yet millions of women remain overdue for recommended tests. This collaboration is designed to help address persistent cervical cancer screening gaps by bringing more accessible screening options to patients across the United States. Labcorp will provide these HPV testing options to support its clinician programs, Gaps in Care health plan programs, and Labcorp OnDemand consumer channel.2-8 “Barriers such as privacy, access, and socioeconomic factors can make it difficult to stay current with cervical cancer screening,” said Jeff Andrews, M.D., FRCSC, Vice President of Medical Affairs, Waters Advanced Diagnostics, Waters Corporation.5-7 “We are at the start of a new era in which screening can extend beyond the clinic, enable more personalized risk assessment, and reach people who have historically been underserved. By offering greater flexibility in how and where people are screened, our collaboration marks a critical step forward in bridging one of today’s most profound care gaps.” The Most Comprehensive FDA-Approved HPV Testing Option The BD Onclarity HPV Assay is the only FDA-approved HPV test that supports all American Society for Colposcopy and Cervical Pathology (ASCCP) Enduring Risk-Based Management Guidelines.2,9 “Cervical cancer screening saves lives, but too many women still face barriers to getting screened,” said Dr. Brian Caveney, Chief Medical and Scientific Officer, Labcorp. “By expanding access and options for comprehensive FDA-approved HPV testing, we can help more women stay current with recommended screening, reach those who may be overdue for care, and support earlier identification of cervical cancer risk.” Certain HPV genotypes, including types 16, 18 and 45, are associated with an increased risk of cervical cancer, making genotype-specific information important for patient management.9 As HPV vaccination has reduced infections from HPV types 16 and 18, other high-risk HPV strains now account for a growing share of cervical disease, particularly among younger, vaccinated populations.10 The BD Onclarity HPV Assay offers extended genotyping that individually identifies HPV types 16, 18, 31, 45, 51 and 52 along with three sets of strategically pooled results, regardless of collection method, making it the most comprehensive HPV screening tool available in the U.S. today.2,11 Waters and Labcorp intend to offer the BD Onclarity HPV Assay by the end of 2026. To learn more, visit https://womenshealth.labcorp.com/providers/cervical-cancer-screening. About Labcorp Labcorp (NYSE: LH) is a global leader of innovative and comprehensive laboratory services that helps doctors, hospitals, pharmaceutical companies, researchers and patients make clear and confident decisions. We provide insights and advance science to improve health and improve lives through our unparalleled diagnostics and drug development laboratory capabilities. The company’s nearly 71,000 employees serve clients in approximately 100 countries, provided support for more than 85% of the new drugs and therapeutic products approved by the FDA in 2025 and performed more than 750 million tests for patients around the world. Learn more at www.labcorp.com About Waters Corporation Waters Corporation (NYSE: WAT) is a global leader in life sciences and diagnostics, dedicated to accelerating the benefits of pioneering science through analytical technologies, informatics, and service. With a focus on regulated, high-volume testing environments, our innovative portfolio harnesses deep scientific expertise across chemistry, physics, and biology. We collaborate with customers around the world to advance the release of effective, high-quality medicines, ensure the safety of food and water, and drive better patient outcomes by detecting diseases earlier, managing routine infections, and combating antibiotic resistance. Through a shared culture of relentless innovation, our passionate team of ~15,000 colleagues turn scientific challenges into breakthroughs that improve lives worldwide. For more information, please visit www.waters.com/about. Disclaimer The BD Biosciences and BD Diagnostic Solutions businesses have been acquired by Waters Corporation (“Waters”). Becton, Dickinson and Company or one of its affiliates or subsidiaries (“BD”) remains the legal manufacturer of Biosciences and Diagnostic Solutions products until all required regulatory transfers are completed. During this interim period, BD maintains full responsibility for all regulatory obligations of the legal manufacturer. Product information provided here is supplied under BD’s regulatory authority. content_title: HPV prevention, local action drive push for a cervical cancer-free Philippines
content: CERVICAL cancer is one of the few cancers the world has set out to eliminate as a public health problem. For the Philippines, however, reaching that goal will depend not only on national targets but on whether prevention actually reaches girls and women in their communities. At the center of prevention is the human papillomavirus (HPV), a common virus transmitted through sexual contact. While most HPV infections clear on their own, persistent infection with high-risk HPV types can lead to cervical cancer. Around 95 percent of cervical cancer cases are linked to persistent high-risk HPV infection, making HPV vaccination an important opportunity to prevent the disease before it develops, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). The WHO has set a 90-70-90 strategy toward cervical cancer elimination by 2030: 90 percent of girls fully vaccinated against HPV by age 15, 70 percent of women screened with a high-performance test by ages 35 and 45, and 90 percent of women identified with cervical disease receiving treatment. At the recent Association of Municipal Health Officers of the Philippines symposium on “Leading Disease Prevention at the Local Level: The Role of LGUs in Protecting Communities,” health experts brought the global target closer to home: how can proven prevention measures translate into protection that people can actually access in their barangays, municipalities and cities? Closing the gaps in HPV vaccination Get the latest news delivered to your inbox Sign up for The Manila Times newsletters By signing up with an email address, I acknowledge that I have read and agree to the Terms of Service and Privacy Policy . Pediatric Infectious Disease Specialist Dr. Fejelia Faulan, resource speaker and panelist, emphasized that gaps in HPV vaccination cannot be traced to one factor alone. Families, health care providers, schools and communities can all influence whether eligible children ultimately receive protection. ADVOCATING HPV VACCINATION Dr. Fejelia Faulan discusses the role of HPV vaccination and stronger local implementation in accelerating the Philippines’ progress toward cervical cancer elimination. “The gaps are on many sides,” Faulan said, pointing to challenges ranging from parental and community attitudes to vaccine access and hesitancy. She noted that misinformation and resistance to vaccination can make reaching eligible populations particularly difficult. Another important gap is data. While government vaccination programs capture vaccinations delivered through the public sector, Faulan noted that there is no comprehensive national registry capturing HPV vaccination delivered through private practice. In Western Visayas, members of the Philippine Pediatric Society have started gathering vaccination information from private practitioners, which Faulan said could help provide a more complete picture of coverage. “We started that program because we wanted to share our data with the government; so that we can address and minimize the gap,” Faulan said. “We hope that there will be others, other municipalities who will join, so that it can become national data for private practitioners.” The issue goes beyond measurement. If local governments do not know how many children have already been vaccinated through private clinics and schools, it becomes harder to identify who is still being missed and where resources should be directed. Faulan also underscored the importance of widening vaccination reach. The current government program prioritizes girls aged 9 to 14, but she noted that HPV infection is not exclusively a concern for women. HPV can also cause cancers affecting men, including anal, penile and oropharyngeal cancers. WHO likewise recognizes HPV as a cause of several cancers beyond cervical cancer. Local success stories show that ambitious vaccination targets are achievable. During the symposium, Faulan highlighted areas that have reached the 90 percent HPV vaccination target, including Banna in Ilocos Norte and Sampaloc, Quezon, while Ilocos Norte subsequently achieved the target province-wide. “If Ilocos Norte has done this, and one municipality in Quezon has done this, I think we can do this,” Faulan told local health leaders. Making prevention a sustained local priority For Dr. Debra Maria Catulong, city health officer of Mandaue City and Best-Practice Panelist, closing the gap requires LGUs to shift their thinking from detecting disease to preventing it in the first place. “Why are we waiting for people to get sick and diagnose or screen? Why can’t we do something before that?” Catulong said, describing Mandaue City's move toward prevention under the primary healthcare approach. CERVICAL CANCER PREVENTION Dr. Debra Maria Catulong shares Mandaue City’s approach to strengthening cervical cancer prevention through local planning, sustainable financing and expanded HPV vaccination.PHOTO FROM The city is putting this into practice through a cervical cancer prevention initiative designed to complement the national program. While government-supplied HPV vaccines reach eligible girls through the public sector, Mandaue City has allocated local resources to extend vaccination to girls aged 9 to 14 in private schools, helping address a population that may otherwise be missed. The city is also working to establish a mechanism for capturing private-sector vaccination data to better understand its actual coverage. For Catulong, however, vaccination campaigns should not become one-time activities. Sustainable prevention requires LGUs to formally incorporate cervical cancer elimination into their annual plans and identify resources that can support implementation over time. Mandaue City, for instance, is augmenting its health budget through several sources, including its general fund, Special Health Fund and Gender and Development Fund. “Marami kayong pwedeng ma-source out na funds. Ang importante lang, the willingness, awareness and acknowledgement na gusto mong ipasok ’yan na budget should be coming from us,” Catulong told municipal health officers. She added that local strategies should combine vaccination with health promotion and navigation for patients already diagnosed, while tapping private companies, civil society organizations and other partners within the community. “It should be something that’s sustainable. As much as possible, embed it in the plans annually,” Catulong said. “Hindi kaya ito ng isang sektor lang. We all need to work together if we really want to eliminate cervical cancer.” That approach reflects one of the central lessons emerging from the symposium: national targets become meaningful only when they are translated into local plans, budgets and services. Science has already established a pathway toward cervical cancer elimination. Closing the remaining gap will increasingly depend on knowing who is still being missed, making vaccination accessible across public and private settings, sustaining local financing and building partnerships that can carry prevention beyond individual campaigns. For LGUs, the opportunity is to turn the 90-70-90 targets from national numbers into something more tangible: girls protected from HPV today, and fewer women facing cervical cancer in the years ahead

content_title: More Adolescents Starting HPV Vaccine Series at Age 9-10 Finish It by Age 13 Than if Starting Later
content: Clinical Hub News & Perspective Tools & Reference CME/CE More EN RegisterLog In Ask AI Search AI Mode Medscape Medical NewsConference News More Adolescents Starting HPV Vaccine Series at Age 9-10 Finish It by Age 13 Than if Starting Later Tara Haelle October 27, 2026 1 Add to Email Alerts Jump to Key Points WASHINGTON — Children whose pediatricians recommended initiating the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination series at ages 9-10 had over twice the odds of starting and completing the series by age 13 than those whose pediatricians initiated the series at ages 11-12, according to a cluster randomized controlled trial presented at IDWeek 2026 in Washington, DC on October 22. “We also found that earlier introduction seems to make HPV vaccine conversations shorter and easier,” Sean T. O’Leary, MD, MPH, professor of pediatrics at the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus and Children’s Hospital Colorado in Aurora, told attendees. “Clinicians currently recommending HPV vaccine at 11 or older should consider earlier introduction, and policymakers should consider a preferential recommendation for earlier introduction of HPV vaccine at 9-10 years.” Currently, HPV vaccination is one of the rare circumstances where the recommendation from the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) differs slightly from that of the CDC, O’Leary said. The CDC recommends the HPV vaccine series begin at age 11 or 12 but noted it can be started as early as age 9. The AAP, meanwhile, recommends starting the series between ages 9 and 12, “at an age the pediatric health care professional deems optimal for acceptance and completion of the vaccination series,” according to the 2018 Red Book. Previous evidence has suggested better uptake of the HPV vaccine when the series is started sooner, but those studies are mostly retrospective, observational studies, and only a small proportion, 2%-8% of adolescents, had initiated the series early. No data existed on the reasons for those early initiation cases, and it’s possible that there are differences between providers who vaccinate earlier vs later, O’Leary said. Similarly, past quality improvement studies that initiated the series earlier generally involved multiple interventions instead of focusing only on an earlier start to the HPV vaccination series. O’Leary noted several reasons it’s worth considering starting the HPV series at age 9, including more opportunities to vaccinate before exposure and a more robust immune response at younger ages. Starting earlier also allows for spreading out the number of shots youth receive since they would then receive fewer shots at age 11, when they are also recommended to get the Tdap and meningitis ACWY (MenACWY) vaccines as well as their annual flu vaccine. Some reports have also suggested that earlier initiation of the HPV vaccine helps uncouple discussions of sexuality from the shot “and allow a better focus on cancer prevention for early introduction,” O’Leary said. “We also know that antibody levels from HPV vaccination are they’re really well sustained, and they plateau for at least 15 years, probably longer.” SUGGESTED FOR YOU The study involved 31 pediatric practices in Colorado and California that currently initiated the HPV vaccine series at ages 11-12. The study randomly assigned 16 of those practices, with 106 clinicians, to receive a training module for clinicians and staff to improve HPV vaccination with specific guidance on wording for parents about starting the series at ages 9-10. The other 15 practices, with 112 clinicians, also received training on improving HPV vaccination but without the specific guidance about ages 9-10. Both arms had Zoom calls annually with feedback on missed HPV vaccinations at visits. The practices’ populations were similar at baseline, with about one fifth of patients on Medicaid and 28% of patients aged 9-13 years up to date on their HPV vaccine series. During the study, the arm focused on earlier initiation had 28,407 patients ever aged 9-13 years, and the control arm had 33,839 patients ever aged 9-13 years. The median age at initiation and completion of the series was 11 and 12 years, respectively, in the age 9-10 arm and 11 and 13 in the age 11-12 arm. Over the course of the study from 2021 to 2026, more adolescents in the age 9-10 arm had initiated the HPV vaccine series by age 13 than in the age 11-12 arm (77.2% vs 67%; adjusted hazard ratio [aHR], 2.19; P < .001). Similarly, 61.7% of adolescents in the age 9-10 arm had completed the series by age 13 compared to 45.1% in the age 11-12 arm (aHR, 2.37; P < .001). Adolescents in the age 9-10 arm initiated the series at a median age of 11 years and completed it at a median age of 11.8 years, compared with a median age of 12.2 years at initiation and 13.3 years at completion in the age 11-12 arm. About 3 months after starting the study, the researchers conducted interviews with 18 clinicians and 17 office staff workers in the age 9-10 arm. They found that many parents seemed receptive to vaccination at ages 9-10, and discussions about the vaccine at these ages appeared shorter with less mention of sexual activity. The main pushback they experienced came from having expected a shot-free visit. “Parents had told the kids they didn’t think they were getting any shots that visit, but lo and behold, yes, they were,” O’Leary said. “Parental questions, concerns, and hesitancy didn’t really appear to differ between the study arms,” nor did the perceived ability to convince parents to get the shot. The clinicians also liked that they could spread out the shots instead of giving them all at one visit. “There was some concern that if you do this in an early visit, maybe they’ll skip later well-child visits,” O’Leary said, but that didn’t happen. “We didn’t see any difference in the percentage of children receiving well-child visits between the study arms, and we also didn’t see a difference in the percentage of adolescents who were up to date on the MenACWY and Tdap vaccines by age 13.” It’s not clear how generalizable to the study might be to states outside California and Colorado or in rural areas since the study clinics were all urban or suburban, O’Leary said. The results of the study were encouraging if not all that surprising, Simon Parzen-Johnson, MD, professor of pediatrics at the University of Chicago and Comer Children’s Hospital in Chicago, told Medscape Medical News. “Most of the conventions that we have in terms of age are somewhat arbitrary, and I think that reassessing and figuring out when the right time is to do things is always a good idea,” said Parzen-Johnson, who was not involved in the research. During O’Leary’s presentation, Parzen-Johnson had asked whether there might be concerns about recommending earlier initiation of the HPV vaccine series in the current climate of increased vaccine hesitancy in the US. O’Leary acknowledged the problems with vaccine hesitancy and confusion about vaccines but pointed out that more than 90% of parents still vaccinate their children on time according to the recommended immunization schedule. While HPV vaccination rates remain suboptimal and have plateaued, they have not declined in the midst of ongoing chaos in the national vaccine conversation, and he doesn’t see a reason for that to change how pediatricians practice. It will take a while to find out how the lawsuit between the AAP and Kennedy resolves and what happens with the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), “so it’s going to be quite a while before we have a functioning ACIP that can be trusted,” he said. “But right now, AAP is taking on these recommendations for adolescents and working with other professional societies.” Parzen-Johnson agrees that current national concerns about vaccine hesitancy should not necessarily affect how individual doctors interact with their patients one-on-one. “Care of children in my mind hasn’t changed from a clinician standpoint, and our goal is always to provide whatever the best care is possible, regardless of what’s going on at a national level, international level, or local level, so I think you can always come back to that,” Parzen-Johnson said. He tells parents that, as a pediatrician, his goal has always remained the same — to take care of their child. “Regardless of what’s going outside of that, we’re always going to be striving to figure out what the best way to do that is,” he said. “So, yes, there’s a lot of noise [in the national discourse], but maybe we should continue to make this about me and you, in this room, talking about your child.” The research was funded by the National Cancer Institute. O’Leary had no disclosures. Tara Haelle has been an independent science and health journalist for more than 15 years, with work appearing in over two dozen trade and consumer publications. She is the author of Vaccination Investigation: The History and Science of Vaccines and The Informed Parent: A Science-Based Resource for Your Child’s First Four Years. Haelle is the public health beat leader for the Association of Health Care Journalists, where she develops resources to help other journalists report on medical studies and public health. She is based in Dallas. Dive Deeper See clinical implications for practice Summarize this article in patient-friendly language 1 What are the clinical implications of this article for practice? content: Search for: Search for: Futurity is your source of research news from leading universities. About Futurity Universities Science Health Culture Environment Videos Interviews Slideshows Audio Science Health Culture Environment Research news from top universities Subscribe 1793372627 New clue hints at how head and neck cancers spread October 30th, 2026 Posted by Washington U. in St. Louis (Credit: Getty Images) Share this Article Facebook Twitter Reddit Email You are free to share this article under the Attribution 4.0 International license. Tags cancer University Washington University in St. Louis Researchers have found that aggressive cancer cells can appear in different locations within head and neck tumors, providing new clues as to why some such cancers—particularly squamous cell carcinomas not caused by the human papillomavirus (HPV)—are more difficult to treat. In research in Nature Genetics, the researchers found two distinct spatial patterns, or locations, where aggressive cancer cells can occur. One location, which was previously known, is at the outer edge of a tumor as cells begin to invade surrounding tissue. The newly discovered location is within the core of some tumors. “Understanding the complex tumor ecosystem with spatial approaches is emerging as a critical tool to study cancer more broadly,” says Sidharth Puram, a professor and head of WashU Medicine’s otolaryngology—head and neck surgery department and senior author of the study. “By using these techniques, we can understand the components of the tumor, but also where those cells are from. In this case, we were quite surprised to see these aggressive cancer cells, which we call partial epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, or EMT, in different locations. It completely upended our views on head and neck tumors.” Head and neck cancers are the sixth most common cancer worldwide, and there is increasing evidence that HPV is strongly associated with a subset of these cancers—particularly oropharyngeal cancers, which include cancers of the tonsils and the surrounding area in the middle part of the throat. The team of researchers studied tumors from patients diagnosed with HPV-positive, as well as HPV-negative, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. By closing mapping where different cells reside within the tumors, the researchers discovered aggressive cancer cells deep inside the tumors of some patients. Further study found that these deeper cancer cells appeared to take on a more aggressive state after interacting with certain immune cells, in response to signals involving a protein called Oncostatin M (OSM). Puram explains that when these aggressive cells were at the edge of a tumor, they were activated by signals from fibroblast cells, which are part of a tumor’s structural elements. However, in the core these aggressive cells were typically found in proximity to concentrations of immune-response macrophage cells that normally digest cellular waste products and foreign substances. These macrophages release the activating OSM signal. “This distinction is critical, as we must target these triggers differently in edge versus core tumors,” he says. “Fortunately, in each case, there are therapeutic agents that are being developed.” While most of the aggressive cells were present at the edge, up to one-third had the more distinct core pattern of distribution in HPV-negative cancers. Notably, Puram says, “We are trying to understand how these different locations affect tumor response to treatment and patient outcomes.” If researchers can figure out how to block the signal or signals that make these cancer cells more aggressive, it could lead to potential new treatment strategies for head and neck cancers. Right now, the research is in its early stages. “It’s a clue,” Puram stresses. “We have an important clue that increases our understanding of how head and neck cancers potentially behave and spread. But it’s significant because it may lead to the development of more effective options to treat some of the most difficult forms of this type of cancer.” Source: Washington University in St. Louis Related Cancer deaths tied to alcohol doubled between 1990 and 2023 ‘Dialogue’ with environment fuels cancer stem cells Head and neck cancers hijack nearby healthy tissue Stay Connected. Show results from: Clear search input Search for result Max Clear search input Search for result Press release “MY CHOICE – A FUTURE PROTECTED FROM CANCER”: Young people turn HPV awareness into peer-to-peer learning 29 October 2026 UNICEF/2026/Moldova/DanBragoi Română English русский Chișinău, 27 October 2026 – Adolescents across all districts of the Republic of Moldova will learn about human papillomavirus (HPV) prevention and the importance of vaccination through the “My Choice – A Future Protected from Cancer” awareness and behaviour change campaign, which aims to build confidence in HPV vaccination. Through interactive games, presentations and peer-to-peer discussions, Youth Klinic Moldova volunteers will share reliable, medically accurate information with their peers, helping them distinguish myths from evidence-based facts. The campaign aims to raise awareness among adolescents about the role of HPV vaccination in preventing HPV-related cancers and to improve access to accurate, evidence-based information for young people and parents. To achieve this, the campaign will mobilize the Youth Klinic Moldova volunteer network, active across 40 youth-friendly health centres, to conduct peer-to-peer awareness activities in schools and communities, including activities involving refugee adolescents. The campaign will also engage young people online through reels, videos, articles and content co-created with adolescents. By using engaging, youth-friendly digital content, including materials developed by young people themselves, the campaign will address common myths, encourage informed decision-making and promote open dialogue and youth participation. Young people and parents who have questions about HPV and vaccination are encouraged to consult their family doctor or visit their nearest Youth Klinic Moldova centre. For information and guidance, they can contact the YOUTH KLINIC SUPPORT LINE at 0 800 800 22. Young people can also submit questions through YKChat, an online counselling service available on Telegram. HPV vaccination is available free of charge in the Republic of Moldova for girls and boys aged 9–26. For children aged 9–14, the vaccination schedule consists of a single dose, while adolescents and young adults aged 15–26 receive two doses administered six months apart. HPV vaccination coverage in the Republic of Moldova remains low. According to the latest available data, just over 46% of girls aged 10–14 have been vaccinated against HPV, compared with approximately 4% of boys in the same age group. Increasing vaccination coverage, alongside screening and timely treatment, is essential to achieving the goal of eliminating cervical cancer as a public health problem. The “My Choice – A Future Protected from Cancer” awareness and behaviour change campaign, aimed at increasing confidence in and demand for HPV vaccination, is implemented by UNICEF, the NGO Health for Youth, and the network of Youth-Friendly Health Centres – Youth Klinic Moldova, in partnership with the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Education and Research, with financial support from the German Government through the German Development Bank (KfW) and the UK Government. Media contacts Valeria Dumitriu Communication Officer UNICEF Moldova Email: vdumitriu@unicef.org About UNICEF UNICEF promotes the rights and wellbeing of every child, in everything we do. Together with our partners, we work in 190 countries and territories to translate that commitment into practical action, focusing special effort on reaching the most vulnerable and excluded children, to the benefit of all children, everywhere. (200 characters max) Your Name: Your Email Address: Send me a copy Personal Message: (Optional) These email addresses will only be used to send out this message. Please wait.. Send Close Online First Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share on X Email Article Copy Article Url Print OCTOBER 30, 2026 More HPV Doses Are Associated With Lower Cervical Cancer Incidence Originally published by our sister publication Specialty Pharmacy Continuum By Marcus A. Banks Two or three HPV vaccine doses are associated with a lower incidence of cervical cancer than one dose, according to a retrospective analysis from the West Virginia University (WVU) School of Pharmacy. The analysis earned a platinum abstract award at AMCP Nexus 2026, in San Diego. manassanant - stock.adobe.com More than 60% of participants in the analysis had received Gardasil 9 (human papillomavirus 9-valent vaccine, recombinant, Merck). The authors are planning subgroup analyses of vaccine type in future work. The CDC recommends that people with robust immune systems receive two doses of the HPV vaccine if the first dose occurs before 15 years of age, or three doses if the first HPV vaccine occurs at 15 years or later. Anyone who is immunocompromised should also receive three HPV vaccine doses, per the CDC. “Not every HPV infection will lead to cervical cancer. Only persistent high-risk HPV infections can result in [the malignancy],” noted study author Saba Dangpiaei, PharmD, MBA, who is pursuing a doctorate in health services and outcomes research at WVU, in Morgantown. “Our results focus on incidence of cervical cancer, not of HPV infection.” Dr. Dangpiaei and her colleagues analyzed the TriNetX electronic health record, associating cervical cancer diagnoses with the numbers of HPV vaccine doses received. This data set is imperfect, Dr. Dangpiaei acknowledged; for instance, someone may appear as having received two doses but in fact they received a third dose that had not been recorded. For their analysis, the WVU researchers included 512 girls and women aged 9 to 45 years, respectively, who received one, two, or three doses of the HPV vaccine. They used propensity score matching to ensure the dose cohorts were comparable to each other in terms of comorbidities. Most patients were white and received their first dose between 18 and 29 years of age. Dr. Dangpiaei and colleagues found that two and three HPV vaccine doses were associated with a lower likelihood of cervical cancer than one dose (two-dose hazard ratio [HR], 0.68; 95% CI, 0.53-0.89; P=0.004 and three-dose HR, 0.54; 95% CI, 0.42-0.68; P<0.001). Every year of delay before receiving a first HPV vaccine dose was associated with higher cervical cancer risk: when one dose was compared with two doses (HR, 1.06; 95% CI, 1.04-1.07), one dose compared with three doses (HR, 1.06; 95% CI, 1.05-1.08), or two doses compared with three (HR, 1.08; 95% CI, 1.06-1.09; all P<0.001). Insurers should support patients receiving two or three HPV vaccine doses, Dr. Dangpiaei advised. “Receiving a higher number of doses of HPV vaccine was significantly associated with lower risk of cervical cancer,” she said. Dr. Dangpiaei emphasized that the results do not imply that receiving a lower number of vaccine doses causes a higher risk for cervical cancer. “In lower resource settings it’s good to receive even a single dose of HPV vaccine. One single dose is way better than no dose at all,” she said. In 2022, WHO announced that a single dose of HPV vaccination could provide comparable protection to two doses, in healthy girls and women aged 9 to 20 years. WHO aimed to simplify follow-up requirements for completing a full vaccine series, which can be expensive. Dr. Dangpiaei reported no relevant financial disclosures. Spec 11 Pages: SP612 Never-Screened Cervical Cancer Rates Climb Among US Women Author(s)Giuliana Grossi Fact checked by: Nicole Canfora Lupo Nearly 1 in 3 women aged 21 to 29 years and 1 in 7 aged 30 to 65 years had never been screened for cervical cancer by 2023. Advertisement Nearly 1 in 3 women aged 21 to 29 years had never been screened for cervical cancer. Image credit: art4stock - stock.adobe.com Nearly 1 in 3 women aged 21 to 29 years had never been screened for cervical cancer by 2023, up from roughly 1 in 8 in 2005, according to a new research letter published in JAMA Network Open.1 The study found the share of never-screened women aged 30 to 65 years also grew over the same period, reaching approximately 1 in 7. Never-Screened Rates Nearly Tripled Among Younger Women Drawing on 9 cycles of the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) conducted between 2005 and 2023, researchers found the proportion of women aged 21 to 29 years who reported never being screened for cervical cancer rose from 12.5% (3.5 million women) to 31.9% (6.2 million women), an average annual percentage change (AAPC) of 5.2% (95% CI, 4.3%-7.5%). The increase accelerated sharply after 2010, climbing at an annual rate of 7.9% (95% CI, 6.0%-14.4%) through 2023. Among women aged 30 to 65 years, never-screening rose from 5.3% (4.3 million) to 14.8% (9.2 million), an AAPC of 6.8% (95% CI, 3.1%-12.0%). Additionally, human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination uptake among women aged 21 to 29 years climbed from 5.7% in 2008 to 54.0% in 2019 but remains incomplete. The study authors noted that nearly 8 million women in this age group remain unvaccinated, and almost a third of them have also never been screened for cervical cancer. Recommendations tailored to you Sign in or create an account to see articles, videos, and podcasts matched to your specialties. Sign in or sign up Advanced-Stage Diagnoses Are Also Increasing The researchers paired the survey findings with US Cancer Statistics incidence data from 2001 to 2023, stratified by age and stage at diagnosis. Among women aged 30 to 64 years, both regional-stage and distant-stage cervical cancer incidence increased by more than 2% annually after 2017. Among women 65 years and older, distant-stage incidence has been climbing since 2001. The authors cautioned that the study was not designed to establish a causal link between nonscreening and rising incidence, but rather to generate hypotheses for future research. An analysis of the 2023 NHIS cohort, comprising 8901 women aged 21 to 65 years, found substantial disparities. Among women aged 21 to 29 years, never-screening was highest among Asian women, at 44.3% (95% CI, 32.07%-56.58%), compared with 28.8% (95% CI, 25.07%-32.57%) among non-Hispanic White women. Educational attainment also tracked with screening gaps: 39.0% of women with only a high school diploma had never been screened, compared with 17.1% of those with a master’s or doctoral degree. Similar disparities by race and ethnicity, education, insurance status, and region emerged among women aged 30 to 65 years, with uninsured women and those living in the South facing elevated risk. Screening Guideline Confusion Compounds the Problem The findings track with a broader pattern of eroding cervical cancer prevention identified in other recent research.2 A December 2025 report on commercially insured US adults found that guideline-concordant cervical cancer screening adherence was below 10%, with rapid changes to US recommendations, including the 2012 addition of cotesting and the 2018 addition of primary HPV testing, contributing to confusion among patients and clinicians. That analysis similarly pointed to disparities by race and socioeconomic status as a persistent barrier to consistent screening. The authors of the new research letter called for targeted strategies to address structural barriers among racial and ethnic minority groups, uninsured women, and residents of Southern states, populations that face both lower screening rates and higher rates of late-stage diagnosis and mortality.1 Limitations of the study include its reliance on self-reported screening data, which is subject to recall bias, and the unavailability of HPV vaccination status in national cancer registries. References Sonawane K, Damgacioglu H, Amboree TL, et al. Rates of never receiving cervical cancer screening among US women, 2005-2023. Co-Diagnostics' Joint Venture CoSara Diagnostics Announces Publication of Peer-Reviewed HPV Screening Study Using CoSara's SARAGENE® Test PR Newswire Thu, October 29, 2026 at 8:00 AM CDT 7 min read CODX Follow-Up Biopsies Identified High-Grade Lesions or Cervical Cancer in 12 of 20 HPV-Positive Women, Including a Cohort with Predominantly Negative Cytology Results CoSara to Exhibit at MICROCON 2026, the Annual Congress of the Indian Association of Medical Microbiologists Co-Dx to Host HPV Screening Webinar on November 17 to Support Awareness Across South Asian Markets SALT LAKE CITY, Oct. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Co-Diagnostics, Inc. (Nasdaq: CODX) ("Co-Dx" or "the Company"), a molecular diagnostics company with a unique, patented platform for the development of molecular diagnostic tests, today announced the publication of a peer-reviewed study using the SARAGENE® Human Papillomavirus High Risk (HPV-HR) Test manufactured by CoSara Diagnostics Pvt. Ltd. ("CoSara"), the Company's joint venture in India. The study, conducted by investigators at a local institution in Gujarat, India and published in Infectious Agents and Cancer, highlights the potential role of molecular HPV testing in identifying women who warrant further evaluation, even when cytology results are negative. Investigators used the SARAGENE® HPV-HR Test to screen samples from 625 women aged 30 to 60, collected through hospital and community screening settings in Central Gujarat, India. Twenty women tested positive for high-risk HPV; 18 had cytology results reported as negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy (NILM), while two had low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (LSIL). Subsequent colposcopy and directed biopsy identified high-grade cervical lesions (CIN II/III) in nine women and invasive cervical carcinoma in three. The full article, "Cross-sectional assessment of high-risk HPV prevalence, genotype distribution, and associated socio-behavioural correlates among women in Central Gujarat, India," is available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s13027-026-00796-x. "Expanding access to molecular HPV testing is an important part of strengthening cervical cancer screening, particularly in regions where access to diagnostics remains limited," said Dwight Egan, Chief Executive Officer of Co-Diagnostics. "We are excited to see CoSara's SARAGENE® test used in published research that brings the importance of molecular screening into such clear focus. Our goal through CoSara is to make high-quality, affordable molecular diagnostics more accessible to laboratories and clinicians across India and South Asia." The SARAGENE® HPV-HR Test is a wet-reagent, laboratory-based multiplex real-time PCR assay that detects HPV-16, HPV-18 and a pooled group of 12 additional high-risk HPV genotypes. The test is authorized for testing in India and is not available for sale in the United States. The investigators noted that the findings are preliminary, given the study's design and the limited number of HPV-positive participants, and that larger studies are needed to confirm these findings. Story Continues The report comes as international efforts increasingly focus on expanding access to HPV-based cervical cancer screening. In July 2026, the World Health Organization issued guidance to help countries implement and scale HPV DNA-based screening programs. CoSara's manufacturing presence in India and regional distribution footprint provide a foundation for the Company's efforts to support broader access to molecular diagnostics. Earlier this year, Co-Dx announced the expansion of CoSara's commercial and distribution territory beyond India to include Bangladesh, Pakistan, Nepal and Sri Lanka, supporting commercialization of the SARAGENE® product line subject to applicable regulatory approvals. In January 2026, the Company reported that CoSara's network included more than 40 distributors across India. CoSara will exhibit at MICROCON 2026, the 49th Annual Congress of the Indian Association of Medical Microbiologists, taking place October 28 to November 1, 2026, at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) Nagpur in Maharashtra, India. The five-day congress is expected to bring together hundreds of microbiologists and clinical researchers from across India, along with pathology laboratory leaders and diagnostics industry representatives. CoSara's booth will feature its molecular diagnostics portfolio, including the SARAGENE® product line. Co-Diagnostics is also developing a separate HPV test for the Co-Dx PCR Pro® platform*, extending its development efforts into near-patient molecular testing. The SARAGENE® wet-reagent assay used in this study is distinct from that development program; the study did not evaluate PCR Pro or its HPV test. In recognition of World Cervical Cancer Elimination Day, Co-Dx plans to host a webinar on HPV and cervical cancer screening on November 17, 2026, intended for healthcare providers, laboratory professionals and other stakeholders across South Asian markets. Interested parties may pre-register by emailing info@co-dx.com. *The Co-Dx PCR platform (including the PCR Home®, PCR Pro®, mobile app, and all associated tests) has not been cleared or authorized by the FDA, is subject to review by the FDA and/or other regulatory bodies and is not yet available for sale. About Co-Diagnostics, Inc.: Co-Diagnostics, Inc., a Utah corporation, is a molecular diagnostics company that develops, manufactures and markets state-of-the-art diagnostics technologies. The Company's technologies are utilized for tests that are designed using the detection and/or analysis of nucleic acid molecules (DNA or RNA). The Company also uses its proprietary technology to design specific tests for its Co-Dx PCR at-home and point-of-care platform (subject to regulatory review and not currently for sale) and to identify genetic markers for use in applications other than infectious disease. content_title: Early ctDNA Clearance Linked to Improved Survival With Pembrolizumab Regimen in HPV-Negative HNSCC
content: Clearance of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) during treatment was associated with improved long-term overall survival (OS) among patients with human papillomavirus (HPV)–negative locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) who received pembrolizumab (Keytruda) plus concurrent chemoradiotherapy, according to an exploratory ctDNA analysis of the phase 3 KEYNOTE-412 trial (NCT03040999) presented at the 2026 ESMO Congress.1 In the HPV-negative subgroup, ctDNA clearance at cycle 3, day 1 of treatment occurred in 76.8% of evaluable patients in the pembrolizumab arm (n = 155) vs 66.3% of those in the placebo arm (n = 166). Among patients who received pembrolizumab plus chemoradiotherapy, the 5-year OS rate was 72.9% for those who cleared ctDNA (n = 119) vs 38.9% for those who did not (n = 36; P < .001). Moreover, the 5-year event-free survival (EFS) rates with these respective groups were 63.1% vs 38.2%, respectively (P = .001). In the placebo arm 5-year EFS rates for patients who achieved ctDNA clearance (n = 110) vs those who did not (n = 56) was associated were 48.4% vs 35.5% (P = .011), respectively, with 5-year OS rates being 58.6% vs 48.2% (P = .075). In the pembrolizumab arm of the HPV-negative subgroup, the 5-year OS rate was 70.5% for patients with a maximum somatic allele frequency (MSAF) below the median (n = 106) compared with 55.8% for those with MSAF at or above the median (n = 95; P = .009). The 5-year EFS rates were 58.9% vs 51.2% (P = .086) each of the respective groups. Regarding the placebo arm, the 5-year EFS rates were 48.1% (n = 96) vs 38.1% (n = 108; P = .002) for patients below and above the MSAF median, respectively, and the 5-year OS rates were 58.3% vs 49.5% (P = .01). Overall, investigators noted baseline ctDNA levels as prognostic for both EFS and OS with pembrolizumab benefits seen across ctDNA levels in HPV-negative HNSCC. For those with ctDNA clearance at cycle 3, day 1 and HPV-negative HNSCC, the clearance was predictive for long-term survival with pembrolizumab plus chemoradiotherapy regardless of other common prognostic markers. "However, [these] results should be interpreted with caution as the HPV-positive group sample size was small,” said lead study author Jean-Pascal Machiels, MD, PhD, in a presentation of the data. Machiels is the head of Adult and Pediatric Oncology at Institut Roi Albert II, Cliniques universitaires Saint-Luc, UCLouvain in Brusselsm Belgium. How was the ctDNA analysis of the phase 3 KEYNOTE-412 trial designed? The trial enrolled patients with evaluable tumor burden per RECIST 1.1 criteria and an ECOG performance status of 0 or 1, in addition to those who had not received prior surgical debulking for the head and neck.2 If patients received prior anti–PD-1, anti–PD-L1, anti–PD-L2 therapy, received a live vaccine within 30 days of their first dose, had active hepatitis B or C or had cancer outside oropharynx, larynx or oral cavity they were not enrolled in the trial. KEYNOTE-412 randomly assigned 804 patients with unresected, high-risk locally advanced HNSCC to pembrolizumab or placebo plus chemotherapy. Patients received pembrolizumab at 200 mg intravenously every 3 weeks for 3 doses with 6 to 7 weeks of chemoradiotherapy, followed by 14 maintenance doses, or placebo on the same schedule. Randomization was stratified by radiotherapy regimen, tumor site/p16 status, and disease stage (III vs IV). EFS was the primary end point of the trial, compared with OS, which was the key secondary end point, and safety was the other secondary end point. Approximately 95% of patients had detectable ctDNA at baseline regardless of HPV status or treatment arm, and baseline ctDNA levels demonstrated a moderate positive correlation with target tumor lesion size in HPV-negative (ρ = 0.494; n = 405) and HPV-positive (ρ = 0.341; n = 166) disease. Did pembrolizumab benefit patients with HPV-negative HNSCC regardless of baseline ctDNA level? In the HPV-negative subgroup, EFS and OS numerically favored pembrolizumab plus chemoradiotherapy over placebo plus chemoradiotherapy at both baseline ctDNA levels. Among patients with MSAF at or above the median in the pembrolizumab arm compared with the placebo arm, the hazard ratio (HR) for EFS was 0.75 (95% CI, 0.52-1.07) and the HR for OS was 0.85 (95% CI, 0.57-1.25). Among those with MSAF below the median, the respective HRs were 0.76 (95% CI, 0.51-1.13) and 0.73 (95% CI, 0.46-1.14). Notably, association between ctDNA clearance at cycle 3, day 1 and outcomes in HPV-negative disease was independent of ECOG performance status and other prognostic markers, including tumor size, disease stage, PD-L1 combined positive score, T-cell–inflamed gene expression profile, and tumor mutational burden. How were ctDNA levels and clearance associated with outcomes in HPV-positive HNSCC in KEYNOTE-412? In the HPV-positive subgroup, baseline ctDNA levels were not prognostic for EFS in the pembrolizumab or placebo arm, or for OS in either arm, and outcomes were similar between arms regardless of ctDNA level. ctDNA clearance at cycle 3, day 1 occurred in 81.5% of HPV-positive patients in the pembrolizumab arm (n = 65) vs 64.6% of those in the placebo arm (n = 65). In the placebo arm, patients who cleared ctDNA (n = 42) had a 5-year EFS rate of 70.2% vs 49.0% for those who did not (n = 23; P = .028). Five-year OS rates for these respective groups were of 85.5% vs 65.2% (P = .013). In the pembrolizumab arm, the 5-year EFS rates were 67.6% for patients who cleared ctDNA (n = 53) vs 41.7% for those who did not (n = 12; P = .095), and the 5-year OS rates were 78.8% vs 83.3% (P = .619). The investigators cautioned that these results should be interpreted carefully because of the small sample size. content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, October 30, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Longer HPV Vaccine Programmes Tied to Higher Coverage Across 31 African Countries by October 29, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Longer HPV Vaccine Programmes Tied to Higher Coverage Across 31 African Countries Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Human papillomavirus vaccination coverage among girls in Africa has risen steadily since the vaccine first reached the continent in 2011, but it still falls well short of the World Health Organization’s target of 90 percent coverage among girls by age 15. That is the central finding of a retrospective analysis of national immunisation data from 31 African countries, published in Discover Public Health, which also reports that each additional year a country runs its HPV vaccination programme is associated with roughly a three-percentage-point increase in first-dose coverage. By 2024, only 31 of Africa’s 54 countries had integrated HPV vaccination into their routine immunisation schedules, mostly targeting girls aged 9 to 14 years. Across the 31 countries, mean first-dose coverage in 2024 was 64 percent, with a standard deviation of 25.5, while last-dose coverage averaged 55 percent, with a standard deviation of 27.3. Those figures represent a modest improvement over 2023, when first-dose coverage averaged 63 percent and last-dose coverage 50 percent. Discover more Check Symptoms African Countries View Census Data The spread between countries was enormous. Five countries exceeded 90 percent first-dose coverage in 2024: Burkina Faso and Cape Verde at 99 percent, Uganda at 95 percent, the United Republic of Tanzania at 94 percent, and Mauritius at 92 percent. Botswana also reached 93 percent for the first dose, though its last-dose coverage dropped to 34 percent. At the other end of the scale, Morocco recorded just 3 percent first-dose coverage, while Gambia and Mali each managed 15 percent, Eswatini 30 percent, and Cameroon and Togo 36 percent. Discover more Buy Maps Africa African countries Shop African Art Regional patterns varied sharply. Eastern and Southern Africa recorded first-dose and last-dose coverage of 77 percent and 61 percent respectively, West and Central Africa reached 63 percent and 60 percent, while North Africa lagged at 52 percent and 27 percent. Only two of nine countries in Central Africa had initiated vaccination, Sao Tome and Principe at 75 percent and Cameroon at 36 percent, and just three of seven North African countries had begun, with Libya and Mauritania at 51 percent first-dose coverage and Morocco far behind. The temporal trend tells a story of early rapid gains, pandemic disruption, and slow recovery. From 2011 to 2016, average first-dose coverage among vaccinating countries climbed from roughly 36 percent to 89 percent, and last-dose coverage rose from about 34 percent in 2011 to nearly 70 percent by 2017. Then came a pronounced reversal: by 2018 and 2019, first-dose coverage had fallen to around 70 percent, and last-dose coverage dropped sharply to 33 percent. The decline deepened in 2020 and 2021, when first-dose coverage fell to about 51 percent and last-dose coverage hit its lowest point at 32 percent. Only from 2022 onward did coverage begin to recover, reaching 64 percent for the first dose by 2024. The authors attribute much of that mid-period collapse to the COVID-19 pandemic. First- and last-dose coverage stood at approximately 70 percent and 33 percent in 2019 but declined to 51 percent and 29 percent in 2020 following widespread disruptions. Because school-based delivery is the primary HPV vaccination strategy in many African countries, prolonged school closures substantially reduced opportunities for vaccine delivery, while health system resources were diverted to the pandemic response. Globally, 23 countries failed to report HPV vaccination coverage data in 2021, compared with only nine in 2019, with several African countries experiencing particularly severe interruptions. To test whether programme maturity matters, the researchers fitted linear regression models relating the number of years a country had implemented HPV vaccination to its 2024 first-dose coverage. The association was statistically significant: the regression coefficient was 2.97, with a standard error of 1.32, a p-value of 0.032, and an R-squared of 0.15, meaning programme duration explained about 15 percent of the variation in coverage. Each additional year of implementation was associated with an increase of roughly three percentage points in first-dose coverage. A sensitivity analysis that removed outlier countries, excluding Cape Verde and Burkina Faso at 99 percent coverage and Morocco below 5 percent, strengthened the estimate to 3.17 percentage points per year, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.85 to 5.5, a p-value of 0.009, and an R-squared of 0.232. Discover more Find Vaccines Book a Checkup vaccines Vaccine vaccine The analysis of vaccination completion revealed a more nuanced picture. Using 2022 data, chosen because 21 of the 31 countries had switched to single-dose schedules in 2023, the researchers found that in the crude model first-dose coverage was not significantly associated with last-dose coverage, with a coefficient of 0.304 and a p-value of 0.070. This suggests that high vaccine initiation does not by itself guarantee completion of the schedule. However, in the model adjusted for programme duration, both predictors became significant: each one-percentage-point increase in first-dose coverage was associated with an estimated 0.32-percentage-point increase in last-dose coverage, and each additional year of programme implementation was associated with an estimated 4.19-percentage-point increase in last-dose coverage. The adjusted model explained 43.3 percent of the variability in last-dose coverage, indicating that programme maturity may support completion through stronger follow-up systems, improved logistics, and better tracking of eligible adolescents. The authors caution that programme duration alone is far from sufficient. A substantial proportion of the variation in coverage remained unexplained, pointing to the influence of delivery strategies, public awareness, vaccine confidence, school enrolment, healthcare infrastructure, financing mechanisms, healthcare worker capacity, and supply chain performance. Previous studies across Africa have identified weak health system capacity, socioeconomic inequalities, vaccine-related stigma, misinformation, concerns about fertility, inadequate health education, and the financial cost of HPV vaccines, often coupled with reliance on external donor support, as barriers to scale-up. Countries such as Rwanda, Uganda, and Tanzania have achieved notable progress through comprehensive school-based programmes, community engagement, and targeted efforts to address sociocultural barriers to acceptance. The study has limitations the authors acknowledge directly. Inconsistent reporting by some countries may have left missing or incomplete data for certain years, and differences in healthcare infrastructure and data quality between regions may affect the accuracy of coverage estimates. The analysis is also ecological, examining associations at the country level rather than following individuals, so the link between programme duration and coverage cannot be interpreted as a proven causal effect at the level of any single girl’s vaccination. Nevertheless, the findings carry practical weight. Sixteen of the 31 countries studied have transitioned to single-dose schedules, which WHO recommends for its potential to reduce delivery costs, simplify logistics, and ease vaccine supply constraints. Political commitment has grown as well, with 43 African leaders signing a declaration in July 2023 committing to vaccinate 40 percent of girls aged 15 and younger by 2025. The authors conclude that reaching the 90 percent target will require sustained investment in health systems, accelerated programme expansion, and intensified efforts against vaccine hesitancy and inequities in access, with single-dose strategies offering an important opportunity to expand first-dose coverage efficiently. D., Etuk, V., Oyedele, O., Osawe, S., Andrew, N., & Okpokoro, E. (2026). Patterns, distributions and predictors of human papillomavirus vaccination coverage among girls across 31 African countries. content: News Issues Wellness Beauty Pharma KOREAN SEARCH Search Health Chosun HPV Genotypes Affect Oropharyngeal Cancer Survival, With Types 33 and 35 Showing Different Clinical Risks by Oh Sang Hun Updated 2026/10/29 09:58 Professor Cha Won-jae of the Department of Otorhinolaryngology at Bundang Seoul National University Hospital, left, and Professor Jin Si-yeon of the Department of Otorhinolaryngology at Seoul National University Hospital. Photo provided by Bundang Seoul National University Hospital. One in four patients with oropharyngeal cancer in South Korea was found to be infected with an HPV genotype other than HPV 16. In particular, patients infected with HPV 33 had a higher cervical lymph node stage, while those infected with HPV 35 had lower overall survival, highlighting the need to pay attention to clinical differences by genotype, a study found. A research team led by Professor Cha Won-jae of the Department of Otorhinolaryngology at Bundang Seoul National University Hospital, with Professor Jin Si-yeon of the Department of Otorhinolaryngology at Seoul National University Hospital as first author, announced on the 29th that it reached this conclusion after analyzing 174 patients with HPV-positive oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma whose genotypes had been identified among those treated at Bundang Seoul National University Hospital between 2003 and 2023. Oropharyngeal cancer is cancer that develops in the oropharynx, the area at the back of the throat, with tonsil cancer and base-of-tongue cancer among its representative forms. Smoking and alcohol consumption were previously considered the main causes, but oropharyngeal cancer caused by HPV infection has increased in recent years. HPV is a virus transmitted through direct contact with the skin or mucous membranes, and some high-risk genotypes can cause cancer if the infection persists. HPV 16 is the most commonly detected genotype in HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer, so previous studies have focused mainly on type 16. However, when the research team analyzed the HPV genotypes of patients in South Korea, it found that 25.3% of all patients, 44 people, were infected with a genotype other than type 16. By genotype, type 16 was the most common at 74.7%, followed by type 33 at 6.3%, type 35 at 4.6%, and types 58 and 18 at 3.4% each. Differences in clinical characteristics and prognosis were also observed according to genotype. Patients infected with HPV 33 had a higher lymph node stage, indicating the extent of cervical lymph node metastasis at diagnosis, than patients infected with HPV 16. Patients infected with HPV 35 had lower overall survival than those infected with HPV 16. The research team explained that the existing perception that HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer has a better prognosis than HPV-negative oropharyngeal cancer is also based largely on studies focused on type 16, making it necessary to examine the clinical characteristics and prognosis of other genotypes in greater detail. In this study, 90.8% of all patients, 158 people, were men. The male predominance was common across all genotypes. The findings demonstrate the need to prevent HPV infection and related diseases in men as well. Professor Jin Si-yeon said, “In addition to HPV 16, various high-risk genotypes, including type 33, were identified at levels that cannot be ignored. If the four-valent HPV vaccine currently used in the National Immunization Program is switched to the nine-valent vaccine, we expect the range of prevention to be expanded further.” The four-valent HPV vaccine currently prevents types 6, 11, 16, and 18, while the nine-valent vaccine additionally covers types 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58. Professor Cha Won-jae said, “As surgical techniques, radiation and chemotherapy, and multidisciplinary approaches have advanced in recent years, HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer has generally shown favorable treatment outcomes. We hope this study will help develop a more detailed understanding of the clinical characteristics and prognostic differences according to HPV genotype.” The study was published in Clinical and Experimental Otorhinolaryngology, an international academic journal in the field of otorhinolaryngology. content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, October 30, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Saudi parent survey finds high childhood vaccination but uneven HPV awareness by October 26, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Saudi parent survey finds high childhood vaccination but uneven HPV awareness Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A cross-sectional online survey of 513 parents in Saudi Arabia found high self-reported childhood vaccination coverage but less uniform awareness of and willingness to recommend human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination. Overall, 98.8% of respondents said their children had received routine vaccinations, and 90.6% reported completing the recommended vaccinations. General vaccine awareness was reported by 96.9%, while awareness of national immunization programs was reported by 57.9%. Among the parents surveyed, 68.6% said they were aware of the HPV vaccine, 52.4% said they would recommend HPV vaccination for their child, and 19.1% selected “I don’t know” when asked about making a recommendation. Researchers conducted the survey from June to July 2025 using an Arabic questionnaire adapted to examine vaccination awareness and perceptions, sources of vaccination information, parent-reported vaccination practices and experiences, and awareness of national immunization programs. Two HPV-specific questions assessed awareness of the vaccine and recommendation intention. The investigators used descriptive analyses, chi-square tests and Fisher’s exact tests for group comparisons. They also fitted a multivariable binary logistic regression to examine factors associated with HPV vaccine awareness and an exploratory multinomial logistic regression to compare different recommendation intentions. Because the study was observational, cross-sectional and based on self-reports through an online questionnaire, it describes reported attitudes and behaviors rather than independently verified vaccination records, and its associations cannot establish that any measured factor caused awareness or recommendation intention. Discover more Book a Checkup Find Vaccines Find Family Lawyer child children Health workers were the most frequently selected source of vaccination information, selected by 60.0% of respondents. The survey also found that 61.4% of parents reported being satisfied with vaccination information in the media. The source questions concerned vaccination information generally and did not separately establish which sources parents used for HPV vaccination. The data therefore do not support treating the health-worker finding as a direct measure of HPV information-seeking or as evidence about the adequacy of public coverage. Adjusted analysis found several characteristics associated with HPV vaccine awareness. Female respondents had higher odds of reporting awareness than male respondents, with an adjusted odds ratio of 1.87 and a 95% confidence interval of 1.23–2.86. Parents in every other region included in the analysis had higher adjusted odds of awareness than parents in the Southern region, with adjusted odds ratios ranging from 2.02 to 3.38 across the regional comparisons. These are cross-sectional geographic associations, not evidence of a decline or improvement over time. Parents who reported problems during vaccination also had higher adjusted odds of HPV awareness, with an adjusted odds ratio of 2.82 and a 95% confidence interval of 1.76–4.51. Parents who expressed either a harmful or non-harmful view of vaccination also had higher adjusted odds of awareness than those who answered “I don’t know” to the general vaccination-view question. In the exploratory multinomial model, HPV vaccine awareness was associated with a lower relative likelihood of answering “I don’t know” rather than “Yes” when asked whether respondents would recommend HPV vaccination for their child. The adjusted relative risk ratio was 0.07, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.04–0.13. Discover more Hire Babysitters vaccine Health Get Health Tips health The estimate indicates a strong statistical association in this sample, but it does not show that HPV awareness caused parents to recommend vaccination. Taken together, the results portray a population in which routine childhood immunization was widely reported, while HPV awareness and recommendation intention were less consistent and included a sizable undecided group. The authors concluded that the findings support stronger provider communication and credible public messaging, particularly for lower-awareness regions and uncertain parents. The study’s online, self-reported, cross-sectional design and the limited number of HPV-specific questions mean that the results should be interpreted as a snapshot of this surveyed population rather than a causal evaluation of vaccine communication or a measure of vaccination coverage across all Saudi parents. Parental perceptions, information sources, and practices related to childhood immunization and HPV vaccine awareness in Saudi Arabia: an observational study. 希腊雅典2026年10月28日 /美通社/ -- 近日,在希腊雅典举行的第38届国际乳头瘤病毒学会学术大会(IPVS 2026)上,国际知名全球公共卫生组织——美国帕斯适宜卫生科技组织(Program on Appropriate Technology of Health,PATH)公布了一项评估九价HPV疫苗单剂接种程序国际III期多中心临床研究的第6个月中期分析结果。数据显示,9-20岁年轻女性接种单剂次国产万泰九价HPV疫苗馨可宁®9后,针对7种高危致癌HPV型别的IgG抗体几何平均浓度(GMC)均显著高于默沙东佳达修®9,且安全性表现总体相近。 7种高危HPV型别免疫应答均高于对照疫苗 加纳纳夫隆戈卫生研究中心(Navrongo Health Research Centre,NHRC)临床科学部主任Nana Akosua Ansah博士是该项研究的主要研究者,她在大会期间公布了由国际知名全球公共卫生组织PATH发起、盖茨基金会资助的新型HPV疫苗单剂次免疫桥接研究(Single-dose HPV Immunobridging Study with New Vaccines I,简称SHINE I;研究编号CVIA 104)第6个月中期分析结果。 该研究是一项在加纳和菲律宾开展的国际多中心、随机、双盲III期临床试验,共纳入1,320名9—20岁女性试验参与者,旨在比较单剂接种国产九价HPV疫苗馨可宁®9与默沙东佳达修®9的免疫原性和安全性。 Nana Akosua Ansah博士公布:单剂接种后第6个月,馨可宁®9针对全部9种HPV型别(6、11、16、18、31、33、45、52、58)的IgG抗体血清阳转率高达95.7%—100%。 针对HPV 16、18、31、33、45、52和58全部7种高危致癌型别,馨可宁®9在9-14岁以及15-20岁两个年龄队列中的IgG抗体GMC在数值上均高于佳达修®9,GMC比值范围为1.38—2.54,所有比值的95%置信区间下限均大于1.0。 对于另外两种非致癌型别,馨可宁®9针对HPV 6的IgG抗体水平在两个队列中同样高于对照疫苗;针对HPV 11的抗体水平略低于对照疫苗,但95%置信区间存在重叠,下限仍满足非劣效。 图片来源:IPVS 2026大会PATH主导的SHINE I研究第6个月中期数据报告现场。 安全性总体相近,研究将继续开展 安全性方面,截至接种后第6个月,两个疫苗组相应年龄队列中的不良事件发生率总体相近,均未出现与疫苗接种相关的严重不良反应,未发现新的安全性信号。 图片来源:IPVS 2026大会PATH主导的SHINE I研究第6个月中期数据报告现场。 万泰九价HPV疫苗馨可宁®9助力全球消除宫颈癌目标 随着全球HPV疫苗单剂接种策略持续推进,如何以更简化的接种程序、更可负担的成本扩大疫苗覆盖,已成为加速消除宫颈癌的重要课题。此次国际多中心研究公布的中期数据,不仅为国产九价HPV疫苗单剂接种的免疫原性和安全性提供了新的临床证据,也展现了中国创新疫苗参与全球公共卫生实践的潜力。未来,随着国产九价 HPV 疫苗更多应用场景下临床数据的积累,将为优化全球HPV疫苗免疫策略、提升中低收入国家疫苗可及性提供科学支持,为实现世界卫生组织提出的全球消除宫颈癌目标贡献不可或缺的新力量。 注:本次公布的是单剂接种后第6个月中期分析结果,研究将进一步考察24个月的免疫原性非劣效临床终点结果。
