title: Quadrivalent HPV Vaccine Shows Sustained Immunogenicity in Women With HIV
excerpt: The quadrivalent HPV vaccine provides durable immune responses and protects against cervical disease in women with HIV.

content: Menu SECTIONS News Features CME Conferences Clinical Tools Special Collections Multimedia DermDx Derm Look-Alikes Fact Sheets Topics Acne Aesthetic Medicine Dermatitis General Dermatology General Medicine Hair and Nail Disorders Infestations and Bites Pigment Disorders Practice Management Psoriasis Rosacea Skin Cancer Skin Infections Skin Injury Vascular Skin Disease Haymarket Medical Network Cancer Therapy Advisor Cardiology Advisor Clinical Advisor Clinical Pain Advisor Dermatology Advisor Endocrinology Advisor Gastroenterology Advisor Hematology Advisor Infectious Disease Advisor Medical Bag MPR Neurology Advisor Obesity Advisor Oncology Nurse Advisor Ophthalmology Advisor Optometry Advisor Psychiatry Advisor Pulmonology Advisor Rare Disease Advisor Renal and Urology News Rheumatology Advisor Sleep Wake Advisor Vaccine Advisor Search for: News Cases Calculators Charts CME Drugs Meetings Multimedia Resources Part of the News and Features CME Conferences Clinical Tools Special Collections Multimedia Share this article Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on LinkedIn Share on Bluesky Share by Email Print Skin Infections Quadrivalent HPV Vaccine Shows Sustained Immunogenicity in Women With HIV Hibah Khaja, PharmD | Publish Date October 26, 2026 Administration of the quadrivalent human papillomavirus vaccine in women with HIV results in durable antibody titers and a low incidence of persistent infections, with viral suppression further protecting against antibody loss. The quadrivalent human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine demonstrates sustained immunogenicity and low rates of HPV-related infection and disease among women with HIV during up to 9 years of follow-up. Continued HIV viral suppression is also associated with a reduced risk for HPV antibody seroreversion. These study findings were published in The Lancet HIV. Women with HIV are at increased risk for HPV infection and associated cervical disease compared with women without HIV. Although previous studies have demonstrated strong initial immune responses to HPV vaccination in this population, data on long-term immunogenicity and clinical outcomes remain limited. Researchers evaluated antibody responses and HPV-related outcomes following quadrivalent HPV vaccination among women with HIV. In this longitudinal cohort study, the researchers recruited girls andSTI women with HIV from 14 HIV and gynecologic care clinics across Canada. The current analysis included participants aged 16 years and older who received the quadrivalent HPV vaccine targeting HPV types 6, 11, 16, and 18. Participants were offered 3 vaccine doses at months 0, 2, and 6, with follow-up conducted from July 2008 through June 2019. Clinical characteristics, HPV antibody levels, cervical cytology, and HPV DNA genotyping were assessed at baseline and at follow-up visits every 6 to 12 months. Immunogenicity outcomes included antibody geometric mean titers (GMTs), seropositivity, and seroreversion. Clinical outcomes included persistent vaccine-type HPV infection, genital warts, and cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or higher (CIN2+). Continued engagement in HIV care to maintain HIV viral load suppression is important in maintaining anti-HPV antibody titres to ensure long-term protection. A total of 353 participants received at least 1 vaccine dose, including 293 in the adult intention-to-treat population and 228 in the per-protocol population. The per-protocol analysis included participants who completed all 3 vaccine doses within 1 year and had no evidence of prior infection with the relevant HPV type at baseline. Among participants in the per-protocol population, the median age was 38.5 (IQR, 32.0-45.4) years, and the median CD4+ count was 499.5 (IQR, 380.8-700.0) cells/μL. At baseline, 160 (70.2%) participants had suppressed HIV viral loads (<50 copies/mL). The population included participants who identified as African, Caribbean, or Black (43.9%), White (36.8%), or Indigenous (11.0%). The median follow-up duration was 5.9 (IQR, 2.3-7.7) years. At month 7, seroconversion rates were 99% for HPV6, 99% for HPV11, 98% for HPV16, and 94% for HPV18. Antibody GMTs initially decreased following the peak response but subsequently stabilized, with sustained antibody responses observed through 9 years. Among women aged 24 to 45 years, antibody GMTs were generally comparable to those reported in a historical cohort of women without HIV. Peak antibody levels were similar between groups for HPV6, HPV11, and HPV18, while peak HPV16 titers were higher among women without HIV. During subsequent follow-up, HPV16 titers were comparable between groups, whereas titers for several other HPV types were higher among women with HIV. In the per-protocol population, seroreversion occurred in 18 of 132 (13.6%) participants for HPV6, 22 of 186 (11.8%) for HPV11, 12 of 141 (8.5%) for HPV16, and 60 of 165 (36.4%) for HPV18. After adjustment for age at vaccination and peak antibody titers, HIV viral suppression during follow-up was associated with a lower risk for seroreversion for HPV16 (hazard ratio [HR], 0.06; 95% CI, 0.01-0.35; P =.0016) and HPV18 (HR, 0.32; 95% CI, 0.18-0.59; P =.0002). Higher peak antibody titers were also associated with reduced seroreversion risk across all 4 HPV types (all P <.0001), while CD4+ counts measured over time were not significant predictors. In the intention-to-treat population, HIV viral suppression was associated with a lower risk for seroreversion across all 4 HPV types, with HRs ranging from 0.10 for HPV16 to 0.64 for HPV18. The incidence of persistent vaccine-type HPV infection was 0.52 (95% CI, 0.22-1.10) per 100 person-years in the per-protocol population, with 6 cases identified during 1151.6 person-years of follow-up. Of these infections, 4 involved HPV18, 1 involved HPV16, and 1 involved HPV6. Participants who developed persistent HPV infection had lower median baseline CD4+ counts than the overall per-protocol population (350.0 vs 510.0 cells/μL). Median CD4+ nadirs were also lower among participants with persistent infection (107.0 vs 230.0 cells/μL). Among participants in the per-protocol population, 4 cases of genital warts occurred during 1089.5 person-years, corresponding to an incidence rate of 0.37 (95% CI, 0.12-0.87) per 100 person-years. No cases of CIN2+ were reported among participants with normal baseline cervical cytology during 1024.5 person-years of follow-up (incidence rate, 0.00; 95% CI, 0.00-0.24 per 100 person-years). In the intention-to-treat population, incidence rates (per 100 person-years) were 1.26 (95% CI, 0.77-1.94) for persistent HPV infection and 1.50 (95% CI, 0.95-2.28) for genital warts. One case of CIN2+ occurred, although HPV16 infection had been documented before vaccination. Comparisons with historical data from women without HIV showed similar CIN2+ incidence rates between groups. However, genital wart incidence was higher among women with HIV in the intention-to-treat and baseline HPV type-naive populations. Study limitations include the small number of persistent HPV infections and cervical disease events, which restricted analyses of associated risk factors. The absence of a placebo-controlled comparison group required the use of historical cohorts, and loss to follow-up may have introduced bias. “Continued engagement in HIV care to maintain HIV viral load suppression is important in maintaining anti-HPV antibody titres to ensure long-term protection,” the researchers concluded. Disclosure: This research was supported by the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR), the CIHR Canadian HIV Trials Network, Réseau FRQS SIDA-MI, and in-kind contributions from Merck Canada. Multiple study authors declared affiliations with biotech, pharmaceutical, and/or device companies. Please see the original reference for a full list of disclosures. This article originally appeared on Infectious Disease Advisor References: McClymont E, Blitz S, Nicolls S, et al; for the CTN 236 HPV in HIV Study Team. Long-term immunogenicity and efficacy of the quadrivalent human papillomavirus vaccine in women with HIV: a longitudinal cohort study. Lancet HIV. Published online October 5, 2026. doi:10.1016/S2352-3018(26)00204-3

content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, October 30, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Parents’ HPV vaccine choices hinge on protection duration and social cues by October 28, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 2 mins read 0 Parents' HPV vaccine choices hinge on protection duration and social cues Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Parental hesitancy remains a major barrier to human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination, and a new discrete choice experiment published in Archives of Public Health offers a detailed look at what actually drives parents’ decisions. The study, made available online as an open-access research article on 28 October 2026, combined a stated-preference survey with an intertemporal choice task to quantify how parents weigh vaccine attributes, how steeply they discount future benefits, and how social signals shape their willingness to vaccinate. In the experiment, protection duration and vaccine effectiveness emerged as the primary determinants of parental choice. Parents also valued social-reference information: they were more likely to choose vaccination when told that healthcare professionals’ own children had been vaccinated. Notably, the vaccine’s origin showed no significant effect on choices. The researchers estimated attribute preferences using a mixed logit model and used latent class analysis to identify heterogeneity, segmenting the cohort into a receptive majority of 79.4 percent and a hesitant minority of 20.6 percent. The study also probed intertemporal preferences by measuring monetary discount rates, a proxy for how strongly people favor immediate over delayed rewards. Interaction models indicated that monetary discounting was jointly associated with the structure of parents’ preferences. However, the authors report that no individual attribute interaction survived adjustment for multiple testing, meaning those attribute-level findings should be treated as exploratory. Interestingly, higher monetary discount rates were associated with membership in the receptive majority rather than the hesitant group. Discover more Find Vaccines vaccine Book a Checkup Read Med Journals Read Bestsellers The authors conclude that parental decisions about HPV vaccination reflect a combination of clinical attributes, social reference information and intertemporal preferences. Because protection duration and vaccine effectiveness mattered most, and because social-reference information about healthcare professionals’ children appeared to encourage vaccine uptake, they suggest that reducing out-of-pocket costs and communicating credible social-reference information are strategies worth testing in future intervention research. Given that the sample was predominantly urban and highly educated, the findings should be generalized with caution. content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, October 30, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Vaginal microbiome shows promise for predicting HPV clearance after HSIL treatment by October 26, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Vaginal microbiome shows promise for predicting HPV clearance after HSIL treatment Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A scoping review of 66 sources finds that cervicovaginal microbial communities dominated by Lactobacillus crispatus are consistently associated with clearance of high-risk human papillomavirus, while dysbiosis marked by bacterial-vaginosis-associated anaerobes or greater microbial diversity is linked to viral persistence and poorer outcomes after treatment of high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions. The findings identify the microbiome as a promising biological correlate of treatment response, but the authors caution that the direct post-treatment evidence remains limited to five studies and does not yet support clinical testing or microbiome-based therapy. Persistent high-risk HPV is the necessary cause of virtually all HSIL and cervical cancer, yet most infections do not produce disease. Approximately 70% to 90% of new high-risk HPV infections clear spontaneously within one or two years, while only a minority progress. The review places this apparent mismatch between viral exposure and clinical outcome in the context of the cervicovaginal microbiome, a community of bacteria and, to a lesser extent, fungi and viruses inhabiting the vaginal and ectocervical mucosa. This microbial ecosystem may influence HPV persistence through changes in acidity, barrier integrity, inflammation, metabolite signaling and local immunity, although many of the proposed causal pathways remain experimental. Research led by Ravel and colleagues established that reproductive-age vaginal communities often fall into five principal community state types. Four are dominated by a single Lactobacillus species: CST-I by L. crispatus, CST-II by L. gasseri, CST-III by L. iners and CST-V by L. jensenii. CST-IV instead contains a diverse, largely anaerobic mixture with depleted Lactobacillus and is associated with bacterial vaginosis. These states are dynamic rather than fixed, shifting over days or weeks in response to factors including menstruation, sexual activity and hygiene. Menopause can also alter the community: declining estrogen reduces glycogen available to support Lactobacillus proliferation, while CST-IV-like and more diverse states become more common in some populations. Discover more Study Anatomy Track Fertility Find an OBGYN Study Biology See an OB-GYN Across observational studies, women with persistent high-risk HPV or more advanced cervical lesions generally carried higher microbial diversity and less Lactobacillus than women who cleared the virus or had no HPV. In an Italian cohort followed for one year, CST-IV was present in 43% of women whose infection persisted, compared with 7.4% of those who cleared it, while Atopobium species were enriched in the persistence group. Another cohort found that decreasing lactobacilli was independently associated with HPV persistence after adjustment for age and menopausal status. Findings from bacterial-vaginosis studies also connected dysbiosis with higher viral persistence and cytological progression. These observations establish an association, but they do not show that microbiome composition itself causes HPV to persist. Laboratory experiments offer possible explanations for the pattern. In cultures of HPV16-transformed cervical cells, L. crispatus and L. gasseri reduced expression of the viral E6 and E7 oncoproteins and downstream p53 and Rb pathways, whereas some dysbiosis-associated bacteria produced contrasting effects. A cocktail containing L. crispatus, L. gasseri and L. jensenii also lowered E6, E7, cyclin A and CDK2 expression in vitro. L. crispatus is distinguished by producing D-lactic acid, which can lower vaginal pH and stimulate anti-inflammatory epithelial responses. Other experiments linked lactic acid to miR-744, a microRNA associated with suppression of E6 and E7 through direct and ARHGAP5-mediated pathways. Dysbiotic metabolite profiles, meanwhile, have been associated with increased TNF-alpha and reduced protective chemokines such as RANTES and IP-10. Proposed effects on cervical Langerhans cells, the antigen-presenting cells that help direct HPV-specific immunity, add another possible pathway, but these molecular results have not yet been confirmed as mechanisms operating in treated patients. Discover more Book a Checkup Find Cancer Care Read Horoscopes The most directly relevant studies concern women undergoing loop electrosurgical excision procedure, or LEEP, or conization for HSIL. Excision removes the HPV-associated lesion but also physically remodels the cervicovaginal niche. In a prospective Italian study of 41 women, four patients who developed persistent infection or CIN2/3 recurrence within six months had nominally L. crispatus-dominated baseline communities but carried unusually high loads of Gardnerella vaginalis, Ureaplasma parvum and Candida albicans. This suggests that co-colonization may distinguish women at risk of failure within an apparently favorable community. A separate Chinese cohort of 26 patients found that microbial diversity fell after LEEP and that pretreatment Lactobacillus depletion was associated with persistent HPV at three months. In 108 women studied around conization, persistent HPV was associated not only with bacterial-vaginosis anaerobes such as Gardnerella and Atopobium but also with Enterococcus and related aerobic-vaginitis organisms, as well as anaerobic and biofilm-forming phenotypes. Perhaps the clearest sign that treatment response and microbiome change are connected came from 85 HSIL patients whose vaginal communities were assessed before and after conization. CST-IV prevalence fell significantly among women who subsequently cleared high-risk HPV, but remained essentially unchanged among those with persistent infection. A Norwegian cohort of 89 LEEP patients and 100 cytologically normal references likewise documented post-treatment shifts and explored whether cone depth influenced associations between microbiota and HPV persistence. Taken together, the direct evidence supports three linked observations: pretreatment dysbiosis is associated with poorer outcomes, excision alters the microbial community, and movement toward Lactobacillus dominance after the operation tracks with viral clearance. The last pattern may be a marker of successful recovery, a contributor to clearance, or both; the available studies cannot distinguish those possibilities. Machine-learning models offer another route to prediction, but none has yet been trained and validated specifically for post-treatment clearance. A study of 272 women identified taxa including Stenotrophomonas, Streptococcus and Pseudomonas as more abundant in HSIL, while Dialister, Bifidobacterium, Faecalibacterium and Bacteroides were depleted, and proposed abundance thresholds as potential screening adjuncts. A separate random-forest classifier built from 33 species separated CIN2 or worse from CIN1 or lower with an area under the curve of 0.952, identifying L. iners as its strongest contributor. Multi-omics work has also suggested that the cervicovaginal metabolome may predict the local microenvironment more effectively than microbial composition alone. These models classify lesion presence or severity, however, rather than viral clearance after LEEP or conization, leaving a major translational gap. Probiotic trials suggest that microbiome-directed treatment might affect HPV outcomes, although the evidence is inconsistent and remains distinct from HSIL treatment studies. In a controlled pilot of 54 women with HPV-associated cytological abnormalities, an oral probiotic drink produced numerically higher HPV clearance than no intervention, 29% versus 19%, although the difference was not statistically significant; clearance of cytological abnormalities reached 60% versus 31%, with p=0.05. A randomized, double-blind trial of oral L. rhamnosus GR-1 and L. reuteri RC-14 in 121 women found no significant difference in HPV clearance, 58.1% with probiotic and 54.2% with placebo, though smear quality improved. Direct intravaginal delivery has looked more favorable: a prospective controlled pilot of L. crispatus chen-01 in 100 women reported lower viral load, higher clearance and improved vaginal inflammation, with sequencing indicating reconstitution of Lactobacillus dominance. Nevertheless, strain, dose, delivery and outcome definitions varied substantially among trials, and no randomized trial reviewed specifically tested a microbiome intervention alongside LEEP or conization. The review’s confidence is further limited by small cohorts, generally 26 to 108 participants in direct peri-treatment studies; inconsistent profiling methods, including microscopy, targeted assays, 16S sequencing and metagenomics; follow-up of only three to 12 months; and limited adjustment for sexual activity, antibiotic use, contraception, smoking and HIV status. Community-state distributions also vary across populations, limiting generalization from any single country or ethnic group. The authors did not pool effect estimates or perform formal risk-of-bias weighting, and their search excluded non-English studies, potentially missing relevant Chinese-language research on post-treatment microbiomes. Future priorities include adequately powered, multiethnic cohorts sampling women before and repeatedly after excision; standardized sequencing and outcome definitions; externally validated prediction models built with post-treatment endpoints; trials of intravaginal L. crispatus as an adjunct to HSIL therapy; and mechanistic studies that directly connect microbial, immune and viral measurements within the treatment window. Until then, the microbiome is a compelling correlate and experimental target, not a clinically validated predictor or therapy. F., Zakumumpa, H., & Chikandiwa, A. (2026). content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, October 30, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health HPV vaccination remains low among young women in Kampala’s urban slums by October 26, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 HPV vaccination remains low among young women in Kampala’s urban slums Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination coverage was low among adolescent girls and young women living in urban slums in Kampala, Uganda, according to a cross-sectional, concurrent mixed-methods study of 290 participants aged 15–24 years. Of the participants, 30.7% reported receiving the HPV vaccine, while 19.0% had completed the two-dose schedule. The most commonly reported barriers were lack of awareness, fear of side effects and limited access to vaccination services. The researchers recruited participants through multistage sampling between August and October 2025. They gathered quantitative data with a semi-structured questionnaire, analyzed the results using descriptive statistics and logistic regression in Stata 16.0, and examined focus group discussions through thematic analysis. The participants had a mean age of 19.76 years, with a standard deviation of 3.00 years. The design captured vaccination status and reported experiences at one point in time, so it can identify associations but cannot establish that particular factors caused low uptake or completion. Discover more Check Symptoms Health health Qualitative findings indicated that knowledge gaps and misconceptions about HPV and vaccination were among the reported obstacles. Parental influence on vaccination decisions also featured prominently in the focus group discussions. Participants described health-system barriers including poor communication, inconsistent availability of vaccination services and negative healthcare experiences. Distance to vaccination sites and limited transport options created additional structural constraints for some residents. These findings explain reported experiences within the study population; they do not establish the prevalence of each barrier across all young women in Kampala’s urban slums. Discover more Find Vaccines Book a Checkup Support Causes Find Housing Two factors were associated with lower adjusted odds of remaining unvaccinated. Participants who lived near a vaccination clinic had an adjusted odds ratio of 0.35 for being unvaccinated, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.21–0.60, compared with participants who did not have that proximity. Those who reported receiving counselling from a healthcare worker also had lower adjusted odds of remaining unvaccinated, with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.19 and a 95% confidence interval of 0.11–0.34. These are adjusted statistical associations rather than evidence that clinic proximity or counselling alone caused vaccination or completion. The study did not test a vaccination intervention or demonstrate that any proposed strategy had increased coverage in Kampala. Its authors identified community sensitisation, improved healthcare-worker communication and expanded community- and school-based delivery as possible approaches to improving equitable access, while stating that further research would be needed to assess their effectiveness in this setting. The results are also limited to the sampled urban-slum areas and to adolescent girls and young women aged 15–24 years, meaning they should not automatically be applied to other age groups, locations or HPV vaccination programs. content: Clinical Hub News & Perspective Tools & Reference CME/CE More EN RegisterLog In Ask AI Search AI Mode Medscape Europe A Single Case of Durable Nivolumab Response in Oropharyngeal Cancer Wolfgang Paik October 26, 2026 0 2 Add to Email Alerts Jump to Key Points Key Takeaways The case involved a human papillomavirus-positive (HPV-positive) squamous cell carcinoma of the oropharynx, staged cT2N2bM0. The patient underwent extensive treatment, including bilateral neck dissection, and later received nivolumab, which resulted in a durable response within 2 months. Despite treatment being stopped because of an adverse skin reaction, the response has been maintained for 4 years. The case report by oncologist Maria Abreu, MD, and colleagues from the Unidade Local de Saúde Lisboa Ocidental in Lisbon, Portugal, documents the potential for a sustained complete response even after discontinuation of immunotherapy. The Patient and Her Medical History A 69-year-old woman presented to a hospital in Lisbon, Portugal, with a sensation of a foreign body in the hypopharynx that had persisted for 10 days. She denied dysphagia, dysphonia, dyspnea, or odynophagia. A history of duodenal ulcer was known. Her regular medications included omeprazole, simvastatin, amlodipine, and valsartan. The family, social, substance use, travel, and allergy histories were unremarkable. SUGGESTED FOR YOU Findings Upon admission, the patient’s vital signs were measured. Respiratory rate, heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation on room air, and body temperature were within their respective normal ranges. Inspection, auscultation, palpation, and percussion of the patient’s body confirmed the information provided in the medical history. A hypertrophic lesion was noted on the left base of the tongue, which was firmly palpable using both hands. Bilateral laterocervical lymphadenopathy was present, with a predominance on the left (particularly at level III). Indirect videolaryngoscopy revealed a lesion affecting the left half of the base of the tongue and the vallecula but sparing the tonsils and lateral pharyngeal walls. MRI confirmed the presence of an oval, primarily exophytic mass in the left base of the tongue measuring 31 × 23 × 22.5 mm, extending inferiorly to the vallecula. The ipsilateral glossoepiglottic fold and the posterior pharyngeal wall were not involved. On the left side, at levels II and III, a cluster of four lymph nodes with a combined short-axis diameter of approximately 5 cm was identified. Following biopsy and histopathologic evaluation, an HPV-positive squamous cell carcinoma was diagnosed. The tumor board classified the tumor as cT2N2bM0. Treatment Induction therapy was followed by chemoradiotherapy. However, posttreatment MRI revealed persistent disease, necessitating extensive surgery, including partial pharyngectomy with tracheostomy, hemiglossectomy, and microvascular flap reconstruction. A bilateral neck dissection was also performed. Systemic therapy with paclitaxel was subsequently initiated. The patient did not tolerate the medication well, so she was switched to cetuximab and methotrexate. Nevertheless, a CT scan performed as part of follow-up care revealed a locoregional recurrence. Hemostatic palliative radiotherapy was initiated. Following immunohistochemical analysis, therapy with nivolumab was started. While on nivolumab, the patient achieved a complete response within 2 months. However, 1 month later, she developed a generalized, difficult-to-treat, itchy rash, necessitating discontinuation of therapy. Surprisingly, follow-up examinations over the past 4 years have shown that the complete response to therapy has been maintained. Discussion “We report a case of durable CR [complete response] in a heavily pretreated HPV-positive oropharyngeal carcinoma, maintained for more than 4 years after nivolumab discontinuation,” wrote the authors of the case report. The case underscores the potential for long-term remission through immunotherapy even in an unfavorable clinical setting. Furthermore, it raises questions regarding the optimal duration of treatment, patient selection, and the potential role of immune-mediated drug side effects as prognostic markers. This story was translated from Univadis Germany, part of the Medscape Professional Network. TRICARE offers options for cervical cancer screening By TRICARE Communications Oct 29, 2026 Oct 29, 2026 0 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Cervical cancer screening is based on your age and risk factors. In addition to cervical cancer, TRICARE covers many other cancer screenings. Talk to your provider to learn about which screening tests may be right for you. Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save FALLS CHURCH, Va. — Knowledge is key when it comes to cervical cancer. There are now testing options that let women screen for cervical cancer risk in a more comfortable, private way. “We know what causes most cervical cancers, and we have the tools to detect and treat changes at a precancerous stage before they can become cancer,” said Dr. Paul Cordts, Chief Medical Officer, at the Defense Health Agency. “This makes it important to know which screenings are recommended for you and when you should get them.” Cervical cancer screening is based on your age and risk factors. In addition to cervical cancer, TRICARE covers many other cancer screenings. Talk to your provider to learn about which screening tests may be right for you. What causes cervical cancer? The main cause of cervical cancer is Human Papillomavirus. HPV is very common, but most people don’t have any symptoms. Certain high-risk strains of HPV cause almost all cervical cancers. Over time, HPV causes changes in the cervical cells that can develop into cancer if they aren’t treated. Early detection is the best defense and saves lives. Know your screening options Prevention: The HPV vaccine is the first step in preventing cervical cancer. Adults up to age 45 can get the vaccine. Screening: Pap tests and HPV DNA testing are two ways to screen for cervical cancer. Depending on your age and medical history, your provider may recommend an HPV test, a Pap test, or both. These tools are a highly effective, proactive approach to get ahead of the disease before any cell changes even occur. New options now available Some military hospitals and clinics now also offer a new self-collection option for HPV testing. This lets people collect their own sample privately during a clinic visit, offering a more comfortable and convenient experience. Costs and coverage You have the flexibility to get the care you need, where you need it, without out-of-pocket expenses. Cancer screening tests are preventive care. This means you’ll have no out-of-pocket costs for covered screening tests. TRICARE Prime and TRICARE Select beneficiaries can access preventive care, including cervical cancer screenings, from network providers in the community at no cost and without needing a referral. What to do See Getting Preventive Care (online at https://tricare.mil/GettingCare/Preventive) for your TRICARE plan’s options. If you need a provider, the Find a Doctor Tool (online at https://tricare.mil/GettingCare/FindDoctor/) can help. Ask your provider about your cervical cancer screening status. Discuss if primary HPV testing or the new self-collection method is right for you. Stay on top of your status. If you’re due for screening, schedule what you need right away. content_title: Molecular HPV Testing Detects Cervical Lesions Missed by Pap Smears, Study Finds
content: Diagnostic Technologies Anatomic Pathology Clinical Chemistry Digital Pathology Flow Cytometry Hematology & Serology Immunoassay Mass Spectrometry Microbiology Molecular Diagnostics Point-of-Care Urinalysis & Toxicology Lab Products Biochemicals & Chemical Reagents Information Technology Lab Automation Lab Equipment Lab Safety Labware & Consumables Quality Systems Disease States Allergy & Autoimmune Cancer Cardiovascular Cerebrovascular Dementias & Alzheimer’s Diabetes & Metabolic Diseases Infectious Diseases Kidney Disease Respiratory Disease Sepsis Womens Health Lab Management Accreditation Company News Compliance Proficiency Testing Resource Center Resources Podcasts Webcasts White Papers Videos Comparison Guides Edition Archive Select Page Study Finds Molecular HPV Testing Identifies Cervical Abnormalities Missed by Pap Smears Oct 29, 2026 | Cancer, Cervical (HPV), Molecular Diagnostics | Researchers found high-grade precancerous lesions or cervical cancer in 12 women who tested positive for high-risk HPV, including several with normal cytology results. A study evaluating the Saragene Human Papillomavirus High Risk (HPV-HR) test found that molecular screening identified high-grade cervical lesions and invasive cancer in women whose cytology results were largely classified as normal. Published in Infectious Agents and Cancer, the cross-sectional study evaluated 625 women aged 30 to 60 across hospital and community screening settings in Central Gujarat, India. Using the multiplex real-time PCR test manufactured by CoSara Diagnostics Pvt Ltd, a joint venture of Co-Diagnostics, researchers identified 20 women who tested positive for high-risk HPV genotypes. Of the 20 HPV-positive participants, 18 had cytology reported as negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy, while two presented with low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions. Subsequent colposcopy and directed biopsy identified high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN II/III) in nine women and invasive cervical carcinoma in three, illustrating the potential of molecular screening to identify high-risk patients who warrant histological follow-up despite negative cytology. “Expanding access to molecular HPV testing is an important part of strengthening cervical cancer screening, particularly in regions where access to diagnostics remains limited,” says Dwight Egan, CEO of Co-Diagnostics, in a release. “We are excited to see CoSara’s Saragene test used in published research that brings the importance of molecular screening into such clear focus. Our goal through CoSara is to make high-quality, affordable molecular diagnostics more accessible to laboratories and clinicians across India and South Asia.” Assay Design and Diagnostic Scope The Saragene HPV-HR test is a wet-reagent, laboratory-based multiplex real-time PCR assay designed to detect HPV-16, HPV-18, and a pooled group of 12 additional high-risk HPV genotypes. The test is authorized for clinical use in India and is not available for sale in the US. Study investigators noted that the findings are preliminary due to the cross-sectional design and the small cohort of 20 HPV-positive patients, emphasizing that larger studies are required to confirm the diagnostic outcomes. Co-Diagnostics also noted that the wet-reagent assay evaluated in the publication is distinct from the HPV test currently in development for its near-patient Co-Dx PCR Pro platform, which was not evaluated in this study and remains subject to regulatory review. Regional Implementation and Screening Initiatives The study findings coincide with growing global efforts to transition cervical screening programs toward molecular testing methods. In July 2026, the World Health Organization released guidance to help member states implement and scale HPV DNA-based testing protocols. To support molecular testing capacity across the region, Co-Diagnostics expanded CoSara’s distribution footprint beyond India earlier this year to include Bangladesh, Pakistan, Nepal, and Sri Lanka, subject to local regulatory approvals. CoSara currently utilizes a network of more than 40 commercial distributors across India. CoSara is presenting its molecular diagnostics portfolio, including the Saragene line, at MICROCON 2026, the 49th Annual Congress of the Indian Association of Medical Microbiologists held Oct 28 to Nov 1, 2026, at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences Nagpur. Co-Diagnostics also plans to host an educational webinar focused on HPV and cervical cancer screening for laboratory professionals, clinicians, and regional stakeholders on Nov 17, 2026. content_title: 国际多中心“头对头”临床研究传来新进展,国产九价HPV疫苗展现硬实力
content: 顶部 首页 首页 晴 / 12° 国际多中心“头对头”临床研究传来新进展,国产九价HPV疫苗展现硬实力 物联 7种高危致癌型HPV抗体水平显著高于进口九价疫苗 近日,在希腊雅典举行的第38届国际乳头瘤病毒学会学术大会(IPVS 2026)上,国际知名全球公共卫生组织——美国帕斯适宜卫生科技组织(Program on Appropriate Technology of Health,PATH)公布了一项评估九价HPV疫苗单剂接种程序国际III期多中心临床研究的第6个月中期分析结果。数据显示,9-20岁年轻女性接种单剂次国产万泰九价HPV疫苗馨可宁®9后,针对7种高危致癌HPV型别的IgG抗体几何平均浓度(GMC)均显著高于默沙东佳达修®9,且安全性表现总体相近。 7种高危HPV型别免疫应答均高于对照疫苗 加纳纳夫隆戈卫生研究中心(Navrongo Health Research Centre,NHRC)临床科学部主任Nana Akosua Ansah博士是该项研究的主要研究者,她在大会期间公布了由国际知名全球公共卫生组织PATH发起、盖茨基金会资助的新型HPV疫苗单剂次免疫桥接研究(Single-dose HPV Immunobridging Study with New Vaccines I,简称SHINE I;研究编号CVIA 104)第6个月中期分析结果。 展开剩余 69 % 该研究是一项在加纳和菲律宾开展的国际多中心、随机、双盲III期临床试验,共纳入1,320名9—20岁女性试验参与者,旨在比较单剂接种国产九价HPV疫苗馨可宁®9与默沙东佳达修®9的免疫原性和安全性。 Nana Akosua Ansah博士公布:单剂接种后第6个月,馨可宁®9针对全部9种HPV型别(6、11、16、18、31、33、45、52、58)的IgG抗体血清阳转率高达95.7%—100%。 针对HPV 16、18、31、33、45、52和58全部7种高危致癌型别,馨可宁®9在9-14岁以及15-20岁两个年龄队列中的IgG抗体GMC在数值上均高于佳达修®9,GMC比值范围为1.38—2.54,所有比值的95%置信区间下限均大于1.0。 对于另外两种非致癌型别,馨可宁®9针对HPV 6的IgG抗体水平在两个队列中同样高于对照疫苗;针对HPV 11的抗体水平略低于对照疫苗,但95%置信区间存在重叠,下限仍满足非劣效。 图片来源:IPVS 2026大会PATH主导的SHINE I研究第6个月中期数据报告现场。 安全性总体相近,研究将继续开展 安全性方面,截至接种后第6个月,两个疫苗组相应年龄队列中的不良事件发生率总体相近,均未出现与疫苗接种相关的严重不良反应,未发现新的安全性信号。 图片来源:IPVS 2026大会PATH主导的SHINE I研究第6个月中期数据报告现场。 万泰九价HPV疫苗馨可宁®9助力全球消除宫颈癌目标 随着全球HPV疫苗单剂接种策略持续推进,如何以更简化的接种程序、更可负担的成本扩大疫苗覆盖,已成为加速消除宫颈癌的重要课题。此次国际多中心研究公布的中期数据,不仅为国产九价HPV疫苗单剂接种的免疫原性和安全性提供了新的临床证据,也展现了中国创新疫苗参与全球公共卫生实践的潜力。未来,随着国产九价 HPV 疫苗更多应用场景下临床数据的积累,将为优化全球HPV疫苗免疫策略、提升中低收入国家疫苗可及性提供科学支持,为实现世界卫生组织提出的全球消除宫颈癌目标贡献不可或缺的新力量。 注:本次公布的是单剂接种后第6个月中期分析结果,研究将进一步考察24个月的免疫原性非劣效临床终点结果。 Free web novels for online reading. 评论 全部 还没有人评论过,快来抢首评 抢首评 推荐阅读 直播:搜狐视频关注流Halloween美剧Cosplay Party 去世不到24小时,人民日报对刘延东的称呼变了,释放三个强烈信号 玩具道道道... 昨天20:26 320.6万+ 健康科普|13岁女孩,接种HPV疫苗正当时 大东北生活... 4天前 7 Dermatologist: The 1 Vitamin You Need for Wrinkled SkinBeauty Guide | SponsoredSponsored Read More Undo 刘欢走了才敢说!杀死他的不是股骨头坏死,而是明知不可为而为之 司徒夜 2026.10.22 71.2万+ 一路走好?刘晓庆凌晨逝世 赵本山灵堂 大衣哥跳楼离世 谣言个个荒诞不经 娱你相遇 6天前 42.4万+ 姆巴佩辱华严重到了什么程度?我们国人要从中汲取什么教训? Madigan Army Medical Center offers eligible patients another option: collecting their own sample for human papillomavirus testing in a private setting. see less | View Image Page JOINT BASE LEWIS-MCCHORD, WASHINGTON, UNITED STATES 10.27.2026 Story by Joseph Jones Madigan Army Medical Center ✔ ✗ Subscribe 3 JOINT BASE LEWIS-MCCHORD, Wash. — Cervical cancer screening can save lives, but discomfort or anxiety about an exam can keep some patients from scheduling care. Madigan Army Medical Center offers eligible patients another option: collecting their own sample for human papillomavirus testing in a private setting. Madigan became the first Defense Health Agency military hospital or clinic to offer HPV self-collection, introducing the option in March 2026. Patients collect a vaginal sample in a private space at Madigan’s pathology laboratory after their provider determines whether the test is appropriate. “We know what causes most cervical cancers, and we have the tools to detect and treat changes at a precancerous stage before they can become cancer,” said Dr. Paul Cordts, chief medical officer at the Defense Health Agency. “This makes it important to know which screenings are recommended for you and when you should get them.” Understanding your screening options Certain high-risk types of HPV cause almost all cervical cancers. HPV is common and often has no symptoms. Persistent infections can cause changes in cervical cells that may develop into cancer over time. Pap tests and HPV tests serve different purposes. A Pap test looks for abnormal cervical cells, while an HPV test checks for high-risk types of the virus that can cause those changes. Depending on your age, medical history and previous results, your provider may recommend one test or both. TRICARE covers Pap tests, HPV DNA testing and HPV self-collection methods. Your care team can help determine which screening method and schedule are right for you. A more comfortable way to get screened Self-collection may help patients who have delayed screening because of discomfort with pelvic exams, a history of trauma or other barriers to care. Madigan patients interested in this option should contact their primary care or women’s health team by phone, during an appointment or through secure messaging in the MHS GENESIS Patient Portal. Collection is available within the primary care and women’s health clinics in addition to the lab at Madigan. A provider will review their medical history and explain the next steps. A positive HPV result does not mean a patient has cancer. It means follow-up evaluation may be needed. Self-collection does not replace every pelvic exam or follow-up procedure, so patients should review their results and recommended care with their provider. Vaccination adds protection HPV vaccination helps prevent new infections with HPV types that cause cancer. Adults through age 26 who have not completed vaccination should ask their provider about catching up. For adults ages 27 through 45, vaccination is an individual decision made with a provider. Vaccinated patients still need recommended cervical cancer screening. Know your coverage TRICARE Prime and TRICARE Select beneficiaries generally pay nothing for covered preventive cervical cancer screenings received from network providers. Non-active-duty beneficiaries can receive covered preventive services from network providers without a referral. Active-duty service members need authorization before receiving preventive care from a civilian provider. Take the next step If you receive care at Madigan and are unsure when you were last screened, contact your care team. Ask whether you are due for screening, which test fits your needs and whether HPV self-collection is an option for you. Staying current on preventive care supports your long-term health and the readiness of the Joint Base Lewis-McChord community. content: Co-Diagnostics' Joint Venture CoSara Diagnostics Announces Publication of Peer-Reviewed HPV Screening Study Using CoSara's SARAGENE® Test Co-Diagnostics' Joint Venture CoSara Diagnostics Announces Publication of Peer-Reviewed HPV Screening Study Using CoSara's SARAGENE® Test PR Newswire SALT LAKE CITY, Oct. 29, 2026 Follow-Up Biopsies Identified High-Grade Lesions or Cervical Cancer in 12 of 20 HPV-Positive Women, Including a Cohort with Predominantly Negative Cytology Results CoSara to Exhibit at MICROCON 2026, the Annual Congress of the Indian Association of Medical Microbiologists Co-Dx to Host HPV Screening Webinar on November 17 to Support Awareness Across South Asian Markets SALT LAKE CITY , Oct. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Co-Diagnostics, Inc. (Nasdaq: CODX) ("Co-Dx" or "the Company"), a molecular diagnostics company with a unique, patented platform for the development of molecular diagnostic tests, today announced the publication of a peer-reviewed study using the SARAGENE® Human Papillomavirus High Risk (HPV-HR) Test manufactured by CoSara Diagnostics Pvt. Ltd. ("CoSara"), the Company's joint venture in India. The study, conducted by investigators at a local institution in Gujarat, India and published in Infectious Agents and Cancer , highlights the potential role of molecular HPV testing in identifying women who warrant further evaluation, even when cytology results are negative. Investigators used the SARAGENE® HPV-HR Test to screen samples from 625 women aged 30 to 60, collected through hospital and community screening settings in Central Gujarat, India. Twenty women tested positive for high-risk HPV; 18 had cytology results reported as negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy (NILM), while two had low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (LSIL). Subsequent colposcopy and directed biopsy identified high-grade cervical lesions (CIN II/III) in nine women and invasive cervical carcinoma in three. The full article, "Cross-sectional assessment of high-risk HPV prevalence, genotype distribution, and associated socio-behavioural correlates among women in Central Gujarat, India," is available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s13027-026-00796-x . "Expanding access to molecular HPV testing is an important part of strengthening cervical cancer screening, particularly in regions where access to diagnostics remains limited," said Dwight Egan, Chief Executive Officer of Co-Diagnostics. "We are excited to see CoSara's SARAGENE® test used in published research that brings the importance of molecular screening into such clear focus. Our goal through CoSara is to make high-quality, affordable molecular diagnostics more accessible to laboratories and clinicians across India and South Asia." The SARAGENE® HPV-HR Test is a wet-reagent, laboratory-based multiplex real-time PCR assay that detects HPV-16, HPV-18 and a pooled group of 12 additional high-risk HPV genotypes. The test is authorized for testing in India and is not available for sale in the United States. The investigators noted that the findings are preliminary, given the study's design and the limited number of HPV-positive participants, and that larger studies are needed to confirm these findings. The report comes as international efforts increasingly focus on expanding access to HPV-based cervical cancer screening. In July 2026, the World Health Organization issued guidance to help countries implement and scale HPV DNA-based screening programs. CoSara's manufacturing presence in India and regional distribution footprint provide a foundation for the Company's efforts to support broader access to molecular diagnostics. Earlier this year, Co-Dx announced the expansion of CoSara's commercial and distribution territory beyond India to include Bangladesh, Pakistan, Nepal and Sri Lanka, supporting commercialization of the SARAGENE® product line subject to applicable regulatory approvals. In January 2026, the Company reported that CoSara's network included more than 40 distributors across India. CoSara will exhibit at MICROCON 2026, the 49th Annual Congress of the Indian Association of Medical Microbiologists, taking place October 28 to November 1, 2026, at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) Nagpur in Maharashtra, India. The five-day congress is expected to bring together hundreds of microbiologists and clinical researchers from across India, along with pathology laboratory leaders and diagnostics industry representatives. CoSara's booth will feature its molecular diagnostics portfolio, including the SARAGENE® product line. The SARAGENE® wet-reagent assay used in this study is distinct from that development program; the study did not evaluate PCR Pro or its HPV test. In recognition of World Cervical Cancer Elimination Day, Co-Dx plans to host a webinar on HPV and cervical cancer screening on November 17, 2026, intended for healthcare providers, laboratory professionals and other stakeholders across South Asian markets. Interested parties may pre-register by emailing info@co-dx.com . *The Co-Dx PCR platform (including the PCR Home ® , PCR Pro ® , mobile app, and all associated tests) has not been cleared or authorized by the FDA, is subject to review by the FDA and/or other regulatory bodies and is not yet available for sale. The Company's technologies are utilized for tests that are designed using the detection and/or analysis of nucleic acid molecules (DNA or RNA). The Company also uses its proprietary technology to design specific tests for its Co-Dx PCR at-home and point-of-care platform (subject to regulatory review and not currently for sale) and to identify genetic markers for use in applications other than infectious disease. content: 头条 湖南 长沙 经济 民生 教育 文体 评论 时事 天下事 游乐 健康 科技 芙蓉区 天心区 开福区 雨花区 望城区 长沙县 宁乡市 浏阳市 湘江新区 关工委 产经 橘洲 夜读 图片 视频 新闻专题 恰同学少年 数字报 EN 健康 惠民减免活动持续!湖南稳步推进HPV疫苗免疫规划落地 稿源:掌上长沙 2026-10-28 15:50 相链区块链 该文章已上链>> 您的浏览器不支持 video 标签。 您的浏览器不支持 audio 标签。 长沙晚报掌上长沙10月28日讯(全媒体记者 杨云龙)记者今日了解到,湖南省正稳步推进HPV疫苗纳入国家免疫规划落地实施,并在免费接种基础上,面向有更广泛防护需求的家庭推出进口九价HPV疫苗惠民减免活动,形成“国家免疫规划保障基础防护、地方惠民政策满足多元需求”的接种模式。适龄人群可以抓住这波惠民福利,为自身的健康增加一份保障。 湖南省正稳步推进HPV疫苗纳入国家免疫规划落地实施,并在免费接种基础上,推出进口九价HPV疫苗惠民减免活动。均为长沙晚报全媒体记者 林暘 摄 抓住免疫“黄金期”,小年龄段接种抗体水平更高 湖南省妇幼保健院妇女保健科主任医师高洁介绍,HPV(人乳头瘤病毒)是导致宫颈癌的必要病因。换句话说,几乎所有的宫颈癌(99%以上)都与高危型HPV持续感染密切相关。在中国,常见的感染型别为16、52、58三种型别。HPV的主要传播途径是皮肤或黏膜的密切接触,其中性接触是最常见的传播方式;HPV也可能通过母婴垂直传播和间接接触污染物品(共用毛巾、内衣等)。 幸运的是,宫颈癌是一种可以预防的癌症,2023年中国《子宫颈癌综合防控指南(第2版)》提出了三级预防策略。其中,一级预防的主要措施包括开展健康教育和接种预防性HPV疫苗。 长沙市雨花区疾病预防控制中心副主任胡蓉介绍,国家明确自2025年11月10日起,将HPV疫苗正式纳入国家免疫规划,为2011年11月10日以后出生、年满13周岁的女孩免费接种二价HPV疫苗,全程2剂次。将低年龄段女孩接种HPV疫苗纳入国家免疫规划,能显著降低未来宫颈癌及其癌前病变的发病率;通过政府主导、免费提供国产二价疫苗,可有效缩小城乡、区域和群体间的健康差距,形成普惠性保障;政策也保留了自费接种四价、九价HPV疫苗的选择空间,提升整体女性健康水平。 世界卫生组织明确推荐:9至14岁未发生性行为的女孩是首要接种人群。从感染风险看,HPV主要通过性行为传播,首次性行为前接种可获得更好的保护效果;从免疫效果看,9至14岁女孩接种后产生的抗体水平是15岁以上人群的2倍以上,保护效果可持续至少10年,仅需接种两剂即可获得长期保护。 “免费+惠民”多元选择,“男女共防”重要性凸显 在国家免疫规划的基础上,湖南又增加了一层福利,推出了进口九价的惠民活动。胡蓉介绍,根据最新的惠民活动细则,9至14岁女性、18至26岁女性及18至26岁男性接种进口九价HPV疫苗,可享受最后一剂次疫苗费用减免,给家长和孩子多一个选择。 适龄人群需于2027年12月31日前完成首针接种,并于2028年6月30日前完成全程接种,方可享受惠民政策。因各区(县、市)惠民活动起止时间可能不一致,具体以当地出台的接种活动细则为准。 由中华医学会妇科肿瘤学分会等七个学会共同制定发布的《预防性人乳头瘤病毒疫苗中国临床应用指南(2025版)》,优先推荐9至26岁女性接种HPV疫苗,其中9至14岁女孩是重点人群;同时推荐27至45岁女性、9至26岁男性接种。 对女性而言,高危型HPV持续感染可导致宫颈癌、外阴癌、阴道癌、肛门癌及口咽癌;低危型HPV则主要引起生殖器疣,虽不致癌,但反复发作,影响生活质量。对男性而言,同样可能因高危型HPV感染引发阴茎癌、肛门癌、口咽癌,低危型HPV也会导致生殖器疣,且男性常为无症状携带者,在不知情中将病毒传染给伴侣。 HPV不仅是女性健康问题,更是全人群的公共卫生议题。高洁表示,按照国内专家共识,HPV防控提倡“男女共防”,男性接种疫苗既能保护自己,也有助于阻断传播、保护伴侣。 专家回应家长疑虑,HPV疫苗越早接种保护效果越好 部分家长担心女孩接种HPV疫苗会影响身体发育,或出现月经提前、推迟、紊乱、痛经加重等问题。高洁表示,依据现有循证医学证据和全球大样本监测数据,HPV疫苗不会影响孩子的生长发育,也不会直接造成月经紊乱。 HPV疫苗属于灭活疫苗,它的作用是刺激机体产生特异性保护性抗体;疫苗不含性激素,不会干扰卵巢功能、骨骼生长以及青春期正常发育进程。全球已有上亿青少年女孩接种,长期监测数据没有发现疫苗会造成身高发育停滞、发育提前或者滞后的情况。 疫苗本身不会直接干扰内分泌、调控月经周期。少数女孩接种后偶然出现单次月经提前或推迟,多与青春期内分泌尚未稳定、接种时紧张焦虑、作息与学业压力等因素相关,属于一过性的周期波动,大多能够自行恢复。 高洁建议,HPV疫苗越早接种保护效果越好,在女孩首次性生活前完成全程接种,效果最佳,早接种、早保护。“总体来说,针对13岁女孩,2价HPV疫苗是全免,进口九价HPV疫苗免一半费用,大家知情、自愿选择。”高洁说,适龄女生及家长可通过当地疾控平台、接种门诊或学校通知等渠道咨询预约。 长沙市华益中学HPV疫苗接种专场,同学们有序接种。 学校与社区联动,把HPV疫苗民生实事做实做暖 国家将HPV疫苗纳入免疫规划,为年满13周岁女孩免费接种,是一项守护青少年健康、惠及千万家庭的民生实事。“作为一名初中校长,也是一名教育工作者,我特别为这项政策点赞。它不只是一针疫苗的事,而是在孩子人生关键期,给她们送上了一份‘健康保险’”。长沙市华益中学党委书记、校长陈婧介绍,学校紧跟疾控、教育、卫健部门节奏,把这件好事做实、做暖。一是快速对接,与社区卫生服务中心点对点对接;二是精准摸底,确保适龄女生无一遗漏;三是暖心组织,坚持“知情、自愿、免费、安全”原则,能用校园专场则用校园专场,能错峰则错峰,尽量减少对正课和家长工作时间的占用。 雨花区黎托街道基成社区卫生服务中心主任严建枚介绍,该中心与辖区学校建立了动态台账,由学工处、校医和班主任共同摸排适龄女生名单。针对家长最关心的“太早”“不安全”等疑虑,该中心通过短视频、班会、家长会和入校宣讲等多种形式逐一回应。接种安排则根据学校教学节奏和家庭时间灵活调整,入校设置临时接种点、在校开设专场、延时接种与周末专场并行推进。首针完成后,该中心按“0至6月”程序对后续剂次实行台账管理;未能在校内完成接种的学生,可在社区门诊补种,周末和延时服务接续跟进,形成从摸排、接种到全程管理的闭环。“辖区接种率能上来,主要是我们和校方把‘家长懂、孩子不怕、流程顺、安全兜得住’这几件事一起协作做实了,接种形式多元化让辖区家庭和学校的负担减少一大截——这就是我们把民生实事办到家门口的本分。”严建枚说。 中国HPV疫苗的全球信任征程-新华网 新华网 > 公司 > 正文 2026 10/27 17:16:15 来源:新华网 从产品出海到能力共建 中国HPV疫苗的全球信任征程 字体: 小 中 大 分享到: 从产品出海到能力共建 中国HPV疫苗的全球信任征程 2026-10-27 17:16:15 来源:新华网 宫颈癌是严重威胁全球女性健康的恶性肿瘤,HPV疫苗接种是世界卫生组织公认的宫颈癌一级预防核心手段。长期以来,全球HPV疫苗供应紧张、可及性不均等问题,始终是广大发展中国家推进宫颈癌消除进程的主要瓶颈。作为中国首款自主研发的HPV疫苗,万泰生物馨可宁®系列依托完全自主可控的大肠埃希菌VLP技术平台,走出了一条从技术突破到市场深耕、再到生态共建的全球化发展路径。 近日,新华网联合万泰生物推出三支分别取景于泰国、印尼、白俄罗斯的短视频,以不同国家的公共卫生实践为切入点,展现着中国HPV疫苗从“被看见”到“被选择”、再到“被信任”的阶梯式跨越。上市七年来,馨可宁®成功通过WHO预认证,全球累计供应超8000万剂,被10余个国家纳入国家免疫规划,也勾勒出中国生物医药产业参与全球公共卫生合作的全新范式。 一针破局:市场验证筑牢信任根基 对于一款疫苗而言,被纳入国家免疫规划,是一国公共卫生体系对其质量、安全性、供应稳定性的最高认可,也是最具分量的市场信任票。在聚焦白俄罗斯的第三支短视频中,镜头以当地公共卫生实践为切入点,通过医护人员的专业讲述和普通家庭的真实感受,展现了HPV疫苗在当地的推广应用,以及民众对宫颈癌预防的认识与期待。这些来自一线的声音,正是中国HPV疫苗融入当地国家免疫规划、助力女性健康保护的生动注脚。 在白俄罗斯,宫颈癌发病率在妇科肿瘤中位居第二,当地公共卫生体系长期面临适龄人群接种覆盖率不足的挑战。2025年,白俄罗斯正式将11岁女孩HPV常规接种纳入国家预防接种计划,中国生产的馨可宁二价HPV疫苗成为该计划的选用产品,为适龄女孩提供免费接种。项目启动仅一年,当地接种覆盖率便超过80%。短视频里受访的当地临床医生表示,宫颈癌是非常严重的公共卫生问题,疫苗接种是最有效的一级预防手段,馨可宁能够针对致癌风险最高的HPV16型和18型提供可靠保护,稳定的供应保障了接种计划的顺利推进。 对于普通家庭而言,这款疫苗也成为守护下一代健康的务实选择。短视频中,陪同女儿接种的母亲坦言,自己查阅了大量专业信息,认定HPV疫苗对女孩的健康成长至关重要。接种完疫苗的女孩笑着说“我原本以为会更疼,结果发现并不疼,一切都很好”,这句朴实的感受,正是疫苗可及性最鲜活的注脚。 白俄罗斯的实践,是馨可宁全球市场认可度不断提升的一个缩影。从南亚到非洲,从拉美到东南亚,越来越多的国家将信任票投给了这款中国疫苗。截至2025年9月,馨可宁二价HPV疫苗已在23个海外国家获得市场准入;2025年1—9月,出口发运量约1500万支,较2024年提升3倍,较2023年提升6倍。从首批疫苗抵达海外机场,到深度融入当地公共卫生体系,这支中国疫苗凭借过硬的品质、稳定的产能,破解了多地的疫苗供应难题,也赢得了国际信任。 一链强基:技术转移深化能力认同 如果说二价疫苗的出海,完成了中国HPV疫苗“产品走出去”的第一步,那么九价疫苗的技术转移与本地化生产,则标志着中国疫苗产业的出海,从“产品输出”升级为“能力输出”。在记录中泰深度合作的第一支短视频里,曼谷的城市天际线、医院接种点的长队、国家疫苗研究所的实验室依次出镜,用三年的时间线串联起从二价疫苗供应到九价技术落地的完整历程。 泰国是万泰推进九价疫苗国际化的重要一站。双方的合作始于二价疫苗的供应:2023年,馨可宁二价疫苗正式纳入泰国国家免疫规划,累计供应超230万剂,支撑当地完成了“100天100万剂”的专项接种行动。接种现场,穿着校服的泰国女生有序排队,医护人员高效登记接种,有效填补了全球疫苗供应缺口下的本地需求。泰国国家疫苗研究所(NVI)负责人Dr.NakornPremsri在接受采访时表示,坦言合作之初泰国HPV接种刚起步就撞上全球供应缺口,正是与厦门万泰的合作,保障了国家免疫规划的实施效果。目前,泰国已有超200万剂中国研发的二价HPV疫苗用于国家免疫规划,90%以上的学龄儿童完成了接种。 二价解决了“有没有”的问题,而更高保护谱的九价疫苗,是全球宫颈癌防控的更高需求。万泰没有选择单纯的产品出口模式,而是开启了深度技术转移的合作路径。短视频中,三方签约仪式的历史影像、九价疫苗生产车间的精密设备、中泰技术人员联合调试的画面依次切换,直观展现了技术转移的全流程。2024年,万泰与泰国NVI、GBP公司签署九价HPV疫苗技术转移协议;2025年,生产工艺验证顺利完成,九价疫苗在泰国实现本地化生产;2026年,九价疫苗泰国上市注册申请正式提交,有望成为国产九价HPV疫苗的首个海外获批市场。从产品合作到技术共建,这条路走了三年多。 合作的深度还体现在科研层面,中泰双方联合开发免疫原性检测方法,国产九价HPV疫苗相关头对头研究结果发表于国际学术期刊《柳叶刀-区域健康》,标志着中国HPV疫苗技术得到国际学术界的专业认可。从产品供应、技术转移到科研合作,中泰疫苗合作不断深化,也为区域公共卫生能力建设提供了新的实践经验。 一心普惠:生态共建共筑健康未来 疫苗的全球化,最终的落脚点是普惠——让更多有需要的人,能够及时、可负担地获得保护。从技术输出到产业生态共建,万泰的全球化步伐,始终围绕着提升疫苗可及性的核心目标,印尼的本土化合作正是这一理念的重要实践。 作为世界上最大的群岛国家,印尼拥有近3亿人口,特殊的地理环境、庞大的人口基数,让疫苗配送与可及性成为当地公共卫生的突出难题。短视频里,印尼食品与药品管理局(BPOM)主席塔鲁纳・伊克拉尔的采访镜头,清晰道出了深化中印尼疫苗合作的核心目标:扩大HPV疫苗覆盖面,加快本土研发与生产能力建设。他表示,印尼有大量女性罹患宫颈癌等妇科癌症,预防这些疾病的关键手段是免疫接种,因此需要高品质的疫苗,特别是九价HPV疫苗,来有效保护人民免受疾病侵袭。 围绕九价HPV疫苗的本土化生产,万泰与印尼Etana公司的合作不断走向深入。不同于常规的技术授权,此次合作以能力共建为核心,双方将工艺参数、质量目标、操作规范、管理体系等全套知识经验完整转移,建立了高度可操作、可复制的本地化生产流程。对于工艺稳健性、质量一致性等核心挑战,双方团队通过透明坦诚的沟通、同步实操培训、联合技术攻关逐一破解。 更长远的价值在于区域辐射,未来,印尼生产的疫苗供给路线将从印尼本土向周边国家延伸。印尼规划将九价疫苗年产能提升至千万剂级别,除满足本国需求外,还带动产品向其他国家辐射,让中国疫苗技术惠及更广泛的区域人群。 三支短视频,三个国家的故事,从不同维度勾勒出中国HPV疫苗的全球化进程。从白俄罗斯的免疫规划准入,到泰国的技术转移落地,再到印尼的产业生态共建,中国疫苗走向世界的方式正在不断丰富。 从二价到九价,从产品出海到技术输出,再到全链条能力共建,这条路径既是中国生物医药产业从“跟跑”向“领跑”迈进的生动缩影,也反映出中国企业参与全球公共卫生合作的方式正在由产品供应向技术共享、能力建设延伸。 公共卫生挑战不分国界,疫苗合作关乎人类共同的健康福祉。在全球加快推进消除宫颈癌目标的背景下,以万泰为代表的中国疫苗企业正携手全球合作伙伴,以中国创新为支撑,以共建共享为路径,为全球消除宫颈癌持续贡献力量,共同构建更可及、更可持续的全球公共卫生未来。 【纠错】 【责任编辑:徐宁】 阅读下一篇: 《了不起的中国传统色》 《AI时代的管理》 《未来人类:科技拓展无限可能》 《残雪》 《相信》 《主角》
